orig_series_arithmetic.description: Recognise equal changes, separate one term from a total, and find every permitted integer index without rounding away a boundary.

sections.title: What makes a progression arithmetic?
sections.label: Terms and equal changes
sections.intro:
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. Each number is a term. In an arithmetic progression, or AP, the change from one term to the next is always the same.

Subtract in the order next term minus previous term. The common difference \(d\) may be positive, negative or zero. For example, \(5,5,5,\ldots\) is an AP with \(d=0\).

blocks.html:
\[u_1=a,\qquad u_2=a+d,\qquad u_3=a+2d,\qquad u_n=a+(n-1)d.\]

The index \(n\) is a positive integer. From term \(1\) to term \(n\) there are \(n-1\) changes.

The points are the terms of \(u_n=9-2(n-1)\). In particular, \(u_1=9\) and \(u_8=-5\).

Only the plotted integer-index points belong to the sequence. Each move to the next index changes the value by \(-2\).

blocks.title: Count the changes, not the terms
blocks.prompt: An arithmetic progression begins \(14,10,6,\ldots\). Find its common difference and its eighth term.

retry.feedback: The eighth term uses \(7\) changes after the first term, not \(8\).

blocks.hint: There are \(7\) changes from the first term to the eighth.

blocks.html: Do not use \(a+nd\) for the \(n\)th term. Substituting \(n=1\) should return the first term \(a\).

sections.title: How do I find an AP from two of its terms?
sections.label: Reconstruct the progression
sections.intro: Write a term equation for each observation. When the indices are not consecutive, do not treat the difference between their values as the common difference: divide by the number of steps between them.

blocks.html:
\[u_j-u_i=(j-i)d\qquad(i\ne j).\]

Subtract to find \(d\), then use either original term equation to find \(a\). Check both observations.

blocks.title: Use the gap between the indices
blocks.hint: Subtract the term equations. The index gap is \(10-4\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[a+3d=17,\qquad a+9d=47.\]
  2. \[6d=30\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=5,\qquad a=2.\]
  3. \[u_{15}=2+14(5)=72.\]

blocks.html: The same idea works for a finite AP when the first and last values are known. If \(d\ne0\), solve \(\ell=a+(n-1)d\) for \(n\), then check that the result is a positive integer. If \(d=0\), every term equals \(a\); the final value alone does not determine how many terms there are.
Label the given indices before forming equations. A gap from term \(3\) to term \(8\) contains \(5\) changes, even though the inclusive block contains \(6\) terms.

sections.title: Why does the arithmetic sum formula work?
sections.label: Add the first terms
sections.intro:
A series adds terms. The prefix sum \(S_n\) means \(u_1+u_2+\cdots+u_n\). It is a total, whereas \(u_n\) is a single term.

Write the same finite sum forward and backward. Every column then has the same total:

blocks.html:
\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=a+(a+d)+\cdots+u_n,\\S_n&=u_n+(u_n-d)+\cdots+a.\end{aligned}\]

There are \(n\) columns, each equal to \(a+u_n\), so \(2S_n=n(a+u_n)\). This pairs two copies of the sum and works for odd as well as even \(n\).
Two copies of \(4+7+10+13+16\) make five columns of height \(20\). Thus \(2S_5=100\), so \(S_5=50\).

\[S_n=\frac{n}{2}(a+u_n)=\frac{n}{2}\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr).\]

Choose the version that uses the information you already know. A negative term or difference does not invalidate either formula.

blocks.title: Use the correct last term
blocks.prompt: An AP has \(a=-3\) and \(d=4\). Find \(u_{10}\) and the sum \(S_{10}\).

retry.feedback: \(33\) is the last term. \(S_{10}\) adds all ten terms.

blocks.hint: Find the tenth term first, then average the first and last terms and multiply by \(10\).

blocks.html: Write the sum formula with your substitutions before giving the total. A calculator can check arithmetic, but the expression shows which terms you added.

sections.title: How do I handle a block or recover a missing term?
sections.label: Prefixes, blocks and differences
sections.intro: A prefix starts at the first term. A block can start later. To keep terms \(p\) through \(q\), remove the terms before \(p\) from the prefix ending at \(q\).

blocks.html:
\[u_p+\cdots+u_q=S_q-S_{p-1}=\frac{q-p+1}{2}(u_p+u_q).\]

Both endpoints are included. The block contains \(q-p+1\) terms.

blocks.title: Keep the starting term
blocks.prompt: An AP has \(a=8\) and \(d=3\). How many terms are there from term \(4\) through term \(9\), inclusive? Find their sum.

retry.feedback: The index gap is \(5\), but the inclusive block contains \(6\) terms.

blocks.hint: The block includes both end terms. Use its first and last values, or subtract \(S_3\) from \(S_9\).

blocks.html: The next \(k\) terms after the first \(k\) have sum \(S_{2k}-S_k\). Subtracting \(S_p\) instead of \(S_{p-1}\) would remove term \(p\) as well.
Two consecutive prefix sums differ by exactly one term:

\[u_n=S_n-S_{n-1},\qquad S_0=0.\]

When a formula for \(S_n\) is supplied only for positive indices, always check \(u_1=S_1\) separately. Do not assume the formula also applies at zero.

blocks.title: Recover the sequence from its sums
blocks.prompt: The sum of the first \(n\) terms is \(S_n=2n^2+5n\), for positive integer \(n\). Find the first term and common difference.
blocks.hint: Use \(u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\), then read the resulting linear term formula.
blocks.solution:
1. \[u_n=(2n^2+5n)-\bigl(2(n-1)^2+5(n-1)\bigr)=4n+3.\]
  2. \[a=u_1=7,\qquad d=4.\]

  3. The given polynomial also has \(S_0=0\), so the difference formula works at \(n=1\).

sections.title: How do I solve for parameters or the number of terms?
sections.label: Equations and integer indices
sections.intro: Terms, prefix sums and block sums can all supply equations in the same \(a\) and \(d\). Write each condition in its own form before solving simultaneously. When \(n\) is known, these equations are linear in \(a\) and \(d\).

blocks.html: If the unknown is the number of terms, the sum formula usually gives a quadratic equation. Solve it fully before interpreting the roots.
A valid number of terms must be a positive integer and satisfy the original condition. Keep every root that passes both tests. Reject negative or non-integer roots; do not round them into answers.

blocks.title: Can both index values work?
blocks.prompt: An AP has first term \(15\) and common difference \(-3\). Find every positive integer \(n\) for which \(S_n=42\).
blocks.hint: Form a quadratic equation in \(n\), then test both roots as term counts.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{n}{2}\bigl(30-3(n-1)\bigr)=42.\]
  2. \[n^2-11n+28=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(n-4)(n-7)=0.\]

  3. Both \(n=4\) and \(n=7\) are positive integers and give the required sum.

blocks.html: A sum need not increase forever. Later negative terms can make an earlier total appear again. Two positive integer solutions can both be correct.

sections.title: How do I find the first index or select terms by value?
sections.label: Thresholds and selected terms
sections.intro:
For a first or last index, solve the required inequality and then apply the integer restriction. Preserve whether the boundary is strict. Check your chosen index and the neighbouring excluded index in the original condition.

The identity \(S_n-S_{n-1}=u_n\) tells you how a prefix sum changes: a positive added term increases it, a negative term decreases it, and a zero term leaves it unchanged. To locate a largest prefix sum in a decreasing AP, identify the last positive term and check whether a following zero creates a tie. If a decreasing AP starts with a non-positive term, the largest sum with \(n\ge1\) is \(S_1\).

blocks.html:
For \(S_n=n(13-n)\), the first plotted value strictly below \(-30\) is \(S_{16}=-48\). The equality \(S_{15}=-30\) is excluded.

For \(a=12\), \(d=-2\), the sum \(S_n=n(13-n)\) reaches \(36\) at both \(n=4\) and \(n=9\). The strict threshold \(S_n<-30\) is first met at \(n=16\).

blocks.title: Check the first successful integer
blocks.prompt: An AP has \(a=3\), \(d=4\). Find the least positive integer \(n\) for which \(S_n>150\), and give that sum.
blocks.hint: Use \(S_n=n(2n+1)\). Check the integer just below your proposed answer.
blocks.solution:
1. \[S_n=\frac{n}{2}\bigl(6+4(n-1)\bigr)=n(2n+1).\]
  2. \[S_8=136\le150,\qquad S_9=171>150.\]

  3. Every term is positive, so the prefix sums increase. The least index is \(n=9\).

blocks.html: A restriction on term values is a different question. First substitute the term formula into the value inequality. Solve for integer indices, then add that selected block. When dividing by a negative common difference, reverse the inequality signs.

blocks.title: Turn value bounds into index bounds
blocks.prompt: An AP has \(u_n=5n-2\), for \(n=1,2,\ldots\). Select all terms satisfying \(18\le u_n<44\). Find the first and last selected indices and the sum of the selected terms.
blocks.hint: Solve \(18\le5n-2<44\), then keep integer indices. Count both end terms.
blocks.solution:
1. \[18\le5n-2<44\quad\Longrightarrow\quad4\le n<\frac{46}{5}.\]

  2. The selected indices are \(4,5,\ldots,9\), giving \(6\) terms.

  3. \[u_4=18,\quad u_9=43,\qquad\text{sum}=\frac{6}{2}(18+43)=183.\]

blocks.html: State what your integer counts: an original term index, the number of terms in a selected block, or the number of terms added so far. These may be different numbers.

glossary.definition: One value \(u_n\) in a sequence.
The position of a term; here it is a positive integer.
The fixed change \(d=u_{n+1}-u_n\).
A sequence with a constant difference between consecutive terms.
The total \(S_n\) of the first \(n\) terms.
Including both stated endpoints.
A boundary value that an inequality requires a term or sum to reach or cross.

examples.title: A decreasing progression still uses the same rule
examples.question: The AP \(9,7,5,\ldots\) continues. Find its eighth term.
solution:
\[a=9,\qquad d=7-9=-2.\]

A decrease is a negative common difference.

\[u_8=9+(8-1)(-2)=-5.\]

The first term is already present; only seven changes are needed.

Counting confirms the sequence \(9,7,5,3,1,-1,-3,-5\).

Negative terms are allowed unless the context rules them out.

examples.title: Two observations determine the whole progression
examples.question: An AP has \(u_3=11\) and \(u_8=31\). Find \(a\), \(d\) and \(u_{20}\).
solution:
\[a+2d=11,\qquad a+7d=31.\]

Each observation becomes an equation using its own index.

\[5d=20\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=4.\]

Subtracting removes the first term; there are five index gaps.

\[a=11-2(4)=3,\qquad u_{20}=3+19(4)=79.\]

Substitute into an original equation, then use the requested index.
Check: \(3+7(4)=31\), as required.

examples.title: A term and a sum answer different questions
examples.question: An AP has \(a=4\) and \(d=3\). Find \(u_{12}\) and \(S_{12}\).
solution:
\[u_{12}=4+11(3)=37.\]

This is one value: the twelfth term.

\[S_{12}=\frac{12}{2}(4+37)=246.\]

The average of the first and last values is also the average of all twelve terms.

\[S_{12}=\frac{12}{2}\bigl(2(4)+11(3)\bigr)=246.\]

The alternative sum formula gives the same total.

examples.title: Remove the unwanted prefix
examples.question: An AP has \(a=5\) and \(d=2\). Find the sum of terms \(6\) through \(12\), inclusive.
solution:
\[\text{Required sum}=S_{12}-S_5.\]

Remove only terms one to five; term six must remain.
\[\text{Required sum}=192-45=147.\]

\[N=12-6+1=7,\qquad\frac{7}{2}(u_6+u_{12})=\frac{7}{2}(15+27)=147.\]

A separate block calculation confirms both the count and total.

examples.title: Subtract consecutive totals
examples.question: The prefix sums are \(S_n=3n^2+2n\). Find a formula for \(u_n\), and hence find \(a\) and \(d\).
solution:
\[u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=(3n^2+2n)-\bigl(3(n-1)^2+2(n-1)\bigr).\]

The two totals contain the same earlier terms; subtraction leaves only term \(n\).

\[u_n=6n-1=5+(n-1)6.\]

Expand the whole bracket before subtracting it.
At the first index, \(u_1=S_1=5\). The sum polynomial gives \(S_0=0\), so the same calculation is valid there.

examples.title: Two prefix sums give two linear equations
examples.question: An AP has \(S_4=32\) and \(S_{10}=170\). Find \(a\), \(d\) and \(u_{12}\).
solution:
\[2(2a+3d)=32,\qquad5(2a+9d)=170.\]

The two sum conditions use different numbers of terms.

\[2a+3d=16,\qquad2a+9d=34.\]

Simplify each equation before eliminating.
\[6d=18\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=3,\qquad a=\frac{7}{2}.\]

\[u_{12}=\frac{7}{2}+11(3)=\frac{73}{2}.\]

A first term or difference need not be an integer.

examples.title: A sum can occur at two different indices
examples.question: An AP has \(a=12\) and \(d=-2\). Find all positive integers \(n\) for which \(S_n=36\).
solution: \[n(13-n)=36\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(n-4)(n-9)=0.\]

\[n=4\quad\text{or}\quad n=9.\]

Both are positive integers; neither may be discarded just because two answers appear.

\[S_4=4(9)=36,\qquad S_9=9(4)=36.\]

Initially positive terms increase the total; later negative terms bring it down again.

examples.title: A strict boundary must be crossed
examples.question: For the same AP, \(a=12\), \(d=-2\), find the least positive integer \(n\) for which \(S_n<-30\).
solution:
\[n(13-n)<-30\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n^2-13n-30>0.\]

Moving every term to one side preserves the exact strict inequality.

\[(n-15)(n+2)>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n<-2\ \text{or}\ n>15.\]

A positive product occurs outside the two roots.
Since \(n\) is a positive integer, the first possibility is \(n=16\).

\[S_{15}=-30,\qquad S_{16}=-48<-30.\]

Equality at the preceding index is not enough for a strict inequality.

examples.title: Select by term value, then add the block
examples.question: The terms are \(u_n=4n+1\), for positive integer \(n\). Find the sum of all terms with \(9\le u_n<30\).
solution:
\[9\le4n+1<30\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2\le n<\frac{29}{4}.\]

Convert value restrictions into restrictions on the index.

The allowed indices are \(2,3,\ldots,7\). There are \(7-2+1=6\) terms.

The upper bound is not rounded to the nearest integer; only integers satisfying it are kept.

extraPractice.title: A progression crossing zero
extraPractice.prompt: The AP \(-7,-3,1,\ldots\) continues. Find \(d\) and \(u_{16}\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the first term and fifteen changes.

extraPractice.title: A last term gives the length
extraPractice.prompt: A finite AP has first term \(18\), common difference \(-2\) and last term \(-20\). Find its number of terms and its sum.

extraPractice.title: Widely separated observations
extraPractice.prompt: An AP has \(u_6=23\) and \(u_{13}=58\). Find its first term, common difference and twenty-first term.
extraPractice.hint: The gap is seven changes.

extraPractice.title: Fractions can stay exact
extraPractice.prompt: An AP has \(a=\frac{7}{2}\) and \(d=\frac{3}{2}\). Find \(S_{12}\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the sum formula without rounding the fractions.

extraPractice.title: A later block
extraPractice.prompt: An AP has \(a=-4\), \(d=5\). Find the sum of terms \(7\) through \(15\), inclusive.
extraPractice.hint: Use nine terms with first value \(u_7\) and last value \(u_{15}\).

extraPractice.title: Decode a prefix-sum rule
extraPractice.prompt: The first \(n\) terms have sum \(S_n=5n^2-n\). Find \(a\), \(d\) and \(u_9\).
extraPractice.hint: Subtract the complete expression for \(S_{n-1}\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[u_n=(5n^2-n)-\bigl(5(n-1)^2-(n-1)\bigr)=10n-6.\]
  2. \[a=4,\qquad d=10,\qquad u_9=84.\]

  3. At the first index, \(u_1=S_1=4\), consistent with the rule.

extraPractice.title: An inclusive boundary counts
extraPractice.prompt: An AP has \(a=5\), \(d=3\). Find the least positive integer \(n\) for which \(S_n\ge98\).
extraPractice.hint: Equality is allowed here. Compare the seventh sum with the sixth.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[S_n=\frac{n}{2}(3n+7).\]
  2. \[S_6=75<98,\qquad S_7=98.\]

  3. All terms are positive, so sums increase. Therefore the least index is \(7\).

extraPractice.title: Sum only the positive terms
extraPractice.prompt: The AP is defined by \(u_n=30-3n\), for positive integer \(n\). Find the last index with \(u_n>0\), and find the sum of all positive terms.
extraPractice.hint: Solve \(30-3n>0\). The zero term is not positive.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[30-3n>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n<10.\]

  2. The allowed indices are \(1\) to \(9\), with first and last values \(27\) and \(3\).

  3. \[\text{Sum}=\frac{9}{2}(27+3)=135.\]

starters.title: Two consecutive blocks
starters.question: The first six terms of an AP have sum \(69\). The next six terms have sum \(177\). Find the first term, common difference and sum of the first twenty terms.
starters.hint: The second condition is a block sum \(S_{12}-S_6\), not \(S_{12}\).
starters.solution:
1. \[3(2a+5d)=69\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2a+5d=23.\]
  2. \[3\bigl((a+6d)+(a+11d)\bigr)=177\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2a+17d=59.\]
  3. \[12d=36\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=3,\qquad a=4.\]
  4. \[S_{20}=\frac{20}{2}(8+19\cdot3)=650.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: express the first block as \(3(2a+5d)=69\).
  • 1 mark: express the next block as \(3(2a+17d)=177\), or an equivalent difference of prefix sums.
  • 1 mark: eliminate correctly to obtain \(d=3\).
  • 1 mark: substitute to obtain \(a=4\).
  • 1 mark: use these values to obtain \(S_{20}=650\).

starters.title: One term and one sum
starters.question: An AP has \(u_5=18\) and \(S_{12}=300\). Find \(a\), \(d\) and \(u_{20}\).
starters.hint: Use one term equation and one sum equation in the same two unknowns.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form \(a+4d=18\).
  • 1 mark: form the correct equation from \(S_{12}=300\).
  • 1 mark: solve for \(d=\frac{14}{3}\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(a=-\frac{2}{3}\).
  • 1 mark: calculate \(u_{20}=88\) using nineteen changes.

starters.title: A total that no integer index reaches
starters.question:
An AP has \(a=11\), \(d=-2\).

  1. Find every positive integer \(n\) for which \(S_n=24\). If there are none, enter “no solutions”.

(b) Find the largest prefix sum and the index at which it occurs.
starters.hint: Write \(S_n=n(12-n)\). For part (a), both algebraic roots must be positive integers. For part (b), inspect when the added terms change sign.
starters.solution:
1. \[S_n=\frac{n}{2}\bigl(22-2(n-1)\bigr)=n(12-n).\]
  2. \[S_n=24\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n^2-12n+24=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=6\pm2\sqrt{3}.\]

  3. Neither root is an integer. Therefore part (a) has no permitted solution; rounding would change the equation.

  4. \[u_6=1>0,\qquad u_7=-1<0.\]

  5. The terms decrease, so prefix sums increase through the sixth term and then decrease. The largest sum is \(S_6=6(6)=36\), at \(n=6\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain \(S_n=n(12-n)\).
  • 1 mark: form \(n^2-12n+24=0\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the two roots \(6\pm2\sqrt{3}\).
  • 1 mark: reject both as non-integer indices.
  • 1 mark: justify the maximum using the change from positive to negative added terms, or equivalent algebra.
  • 1 mark: give the maximum \(36\) at \(n=6\).

starters.title: An index in a selected block
starters.question:
An AP has \(u_n=2n+1\), for positive integer \(n\). Select all terms strictly between \(15\) and \(60\).

  1. Find the first and last selected indices and the sum of all selected terms.

(b) Starting from the first selected term, find the least number \(k\) of selected terms whose sum exceeds \(400\).
starters.hint: The selected terms form a new finite AP. Its first value is \(17\), but its first original index is \(8\).
starters.solution:
1. \[15<2n+1<60\quad\Longrightarrow\quad7<n<\frac{59}{2}.\]

  2. The original indices run from \(8\) to \(29\), giving \(22\) terms, from \(17\) to \(59\).

  3. \[\text{Total}=\frac{22}{2}(17+59)=836.\]
  4. \[T_k=\frac{k}{2}\bigl(34+2(k-1)\bigr)=k(k+16).\]

    Use a new sum symbol to distinguish the selected block from the original prefix.

  5. \[k(k+16)>400\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k>-8+4\sqrt{29}\quad(k>0).\]
  6. \[T_{13}=377\le400,\qquad T_{14}=420>400.\]

  7. The least number is \(k=14\), within the available \(22\) terms. These are original terms \(8\) through \(21\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: solve the strict value bounds as \(7<n<\frac{59}{2}\).
  • 1 mark: identify indices \(8\) through \(29\) and \(22\) included terms.
  • 1 mark: obtain the selected total \(836\).
  • 1 mark: form \(T_k=k(k+16)\).
  • 1 mark: solve the positive-index threshold for \(k\).
  • 1 mark: check \(T_{13}=377\) and \(T_{14}=420\).
  • 1 mark: conclude \(k=14\) and verify that this many selected terms are available.

revision.body:
Identify the index, the required term or sum, and any strict boundary before choosing a formula.

Terms and reconstruction

\(u_n=a+(n-1)d\), with positive integer \(n\). The difference may be positive, negative or zero.

\(u_j-u_i=(j-i)d\). Use the index gap, then substitute to find \(a\).

Prefix and block sums

\[S_n=\frac{n}{2}(a+u_n)=\frac{n}{2}\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr).\]

Forward and reversed copies give \(n\) equal pairs.

\[u_p+\cdots+u_q=S_q-S_{p-1}=\frac{q-p+1}{2}(u_p+u_q).\]

Recover terms and solve conditions

\(u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\), with \(S_0=0\). Check \(u_1=S_1\) if a supplied sum formula is stated only for positive indices.

Write each term or sum condition separately. Keep all positive integer roots that satisfy the original equation; never round a non-integer root into an index.

Thresholds and selected blocks

Solve the inequality, restrict to integer indices, then check the boundary and its neighbour.

Since \(S_n-S_{n-1}=u_n\), negative added terms make sums fall. A zero added term gives a tie.

For terms selected by value, find the allowed indices first. Count both ends with \(q-p+1\).
revision.checks:
• Did I use \(n-1\) changes?
  • Did I distinguish a term, a prefix and a block?
  • Did I retain every valid integer root?
  • Did I preserve strict and inclusive boundaries?
revision.examTip: Did I preserve strict and inclusive boundaries?

orig_series_geometric.description: Use a fixed multiplier to find terms and totals, decide whether an infinite sum exists, and measure exactly what a partial sum leaves out.

sections.title: What makes a progression geometric?
sections.label: A fixed multiplier
sections.intro: In a geometric progression, or GP, each term is obtained by multiplying the preceding term by the same number \(r\), called the common ratio. Let \(a\) be the first term.

blocks.html:
\[u_1=a,\qquad u_{n+1}=ru_n.\]\[u_n=ar^{n-1}\qquad(r\ne0).\]

The index \(n\) is a positive integer. From the first term to the \(n\)th term there are \(n-1\) multiplications.

When the preceding term is nonzero, calculate \(r=\frac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}\). A negative ratio makes nonzero terms alternate in sign. Compare magnitudes using \(|r|\): they shrink if \(0<|r|<1\), stay equal if \(|r|=1\), and grow if \(|r|>1\).

The middle plot uses ratio \(\frac12\) and the right-hand plot uses ratio \(-\frac12\). Both sequences shrink in magnitude. Only the negative multiplier alternates the signs.

The three sequences have the same first term, \(a=4\). Their ratios control growth, decay and alternation. Only integer-index points are terms.

blocks.title: Keep the negative multiplier
blocks.prompt: A GP begins \(-6,12,-24,\ldots\). Find its common ratio and fifth term.

retry.feedback: The fifth term uses the power \(4\), because the first term is already present.

blocks.hint: Divide the second term by the first, then use four multiplications after the first term.

blocks.html: Do not divide by a zero term to find a ratio. For \(r=0\), write the sequence directly as \(a,0,0,\ldots\). If \(a=0\), every term is zero for any chosen multiplier; the zero sequence does not determine a unique ratio.

sections.title: How do I reconstruct a GP from indexed terms?
sections.label: Gaps and paired signs
sections.intro: Write both term equations. If the earlier given term is nonzero, divide the later term by it. The exponent is the number of index steps between the observations.

blocks.html:
\[\frac{u_j}{u_i}=r^{j-i}\qquad(j>i,\ u_i\ne0).\]

Solve for every real ratio, then substitute each into an original term equation to find its corresponding first term. An even power may leave two signs; an odd power has only one real root.

blocks.title: An even gap keeps two signs
blocks.prompt: A GP has \(u_3=20\) and \(u_5=5\). Find all real possibilities for \(r\), and the first term \(a\) that works for both.
blocks.hint: The gap is two multiplications. Both ratios have the same square.
blocks.solution:
1. \[r^2=\frac{5}{20}=\frac{1}{4}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\pm\frac{1}{2}.\]
  2. \[a=\frac{u_3}{r^2}=\frac{20}{\frac{1}{4}}=80.\]

  3. Both progressions satisfy both original observations.

blocks.html: Keep candidate pairs together. When asked for all real pairs first, retain both signs before applying a later condition such as “all terms are positive”. If positivity is given from the outset, it implies \(a>0\) and \(r>0\).

sections.title: Why does the finite-sum formula work?
sections.label: Derive and use finite sums
sections.intro: The prefix sum \(S_n\) adds the first \(n\) terms. Multiply the whole sum by \(r\): each term moves one power along. Subtract the second row from the first.

blocks.html:
\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=a+ar+\cdots+ar^{n-1},\\rS_n&=ar+ar^2+\cdots+ar^n.\end{aligned}\]\[(1-r)S_n=a-ar^n.\]

The middle terms cancel. Only the original first term and the new final term remain.

Take four terms with first term \(3\) and ratio \(2\). Multiply the sum by \(2\) and align equal terms before subtracting.

\[\begin{aligned}S_4&=3+6+12+24,\\2S_4&=\phantom{3+{}}6+12+24+48.\end{aligned}\]

The middle terms cancel on subtraction.

\[(1-2)S_4=3-48\implies S_4=45.\]

For \(a=3\), \(r=2\) and \(n=4\), the matching middle terms cancel. Thus \((1-2)S_4=3-48\), giving \(S_4=45\).

\[S_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}=\frac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}\qquad(r\ne1).\]

These are equivalent formulas. A finite sum needs no convergence restriction.

If \(r=1\), every term is \(a\), so use \(S_n=na\). Dividing the previous equation by \(1-r\) would divide by zero. If \(r=0\), only the first term can be nonzero, so \(S_n=a\) for every positive integer \(n\).

blocks.title: Three finite sums, three ratio cases
blocks.hint: The ratio-one GP is constant. The ratio-zero GP has only its first term nonzero.

blocks.html: A term uses \(r^{n-1}\); the finite-sum formula uses \(r^n\). Identify whether the question asks for one term or a total before substituting.

If a finite sum is given and \(n\) is unknown, rearrange to isolate \(r^n\). Compare integer powers, using a calculator table if helpful. A number of terms must be a positive integer and satisfy the original sum equation.

sections.title: How do I add a block or combine term and sum conditions?
sections.label: Blocks and reconstruction
sections.intro: Terms \(p\) through \(q\), inclusive, form a GP with first term \(u_p\), the same ratio, and \(q-p+1\) terms. Alternatively, remove the prefix before the block.

blocks.html:
\[u_p+\cdots+u_q=S_q-S_{p-1}=\frac{u_p(1-r^{q-p+1})}{1-r}\qquad(r\ne1).\]

Use \(S_0=0\). When \(r=1\), multiply the block’s number of terms by \(a\).
For consecutive blocks of the same length \(k\), each entry in the second block is \(r^k\) times its matching entry in the first. Therefore:

\[\text{next block sum}=r^k\times\text{previous block sum}.\]

You may divide the two block sums only when the previous one is nonzero. For example, with \(r=-1\), a block of even length can sum to zero; the relation remains true, but the quotient is undefined.

blocks.title: Recover a GP from two blocks
blocks.prompt: The first two terms of a GP sum to \(18\). The next two terms sum to \(162\). Find all real ratios, and give the corresponding first term for each sign.
blocks.hint: The second block is the first block multiplied by \(r^2\). Use \(a(1+r)=18\) for each ratio.
blocks.solution:
1. \[r^2=\frac{162}{18}=9\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=3\ \text{or}\ r=-3.\]
  2. \[r=3:\quad4a=18\Rightarrow a=\frac{9}{2}.\]
  3. \[r=-3:\quad-2a=18\Rightarrow a=-9.\]

  4. These are finite blocks; neither ratio is rejected for having magnitude greater than one.

blocks.html: For a term and a finite-sum condition, express both in \(a\) and \(r\). A short sum may be easiest written directly as \(a+ar+ar^2\). Substitute, solve the resulting equation and verify every candidate in both original conditions.

blocks.title: A term and a total can leave two GPs
blocks.prompt: A GP has \(u_2=6\) and \(S_3=26\). Find both possible progressions. Enter the smaller ratio and its first term, then the larger ratio and its first term.
blocks.hint: Use \(ar=6\), so \(r\ne0\) and \(a=\frac{6}{r}\). Substitute into \(a+ar+ar^2=26\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{6}{r}+6+6r=26\quad\Longrightarrow\quad3r^2-10r+3=0.\]
  2. \[(3r-1)(r-3)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\frac{1}{3}\ \text{or}\ r=3.\]
  3. \[(a,r)=\left(18,\frac{1}{3}\right)\quad\text{or}\quad(2,3).\]

  4. The first three terms are \(18,6,2\) or \(2,6,18\); both totals are \(26\).

sections.title: When does a sum to infinity exist?
sections.label: Convergence and infinite sums
sections.intro: A sum to infinity exists when the partial sums \(S_1,S_2,\ldots\) approach one finite value. For a GP with \(a\ne0\), this happens exactly when \(|r|<1\): the power \(r^n\) then approaches zero in the finite-sum formula.

blocks.html:
\[S_\infty=\frac{a}{1-r}\qquad\text{when }|r|<1.\]

Check the convergence condition before using this formula.

For a nonzero GP, \(r=1\) makes the partial sums \(a,2a,3a,\ldots\); \(r=-1\) makes them \(a,0,a,0,\ldots\). Neither settles at one finite total. If \(|r|>1\), the terms do not even approach zero. The all-zero sequence is a separate simple case: its sum is zero for any multiplier.

blocks.title: Apply the convergence condition precisely
blocks.prompt:
Consider these fixed-multiplier sequences:

A: \(a=4,\ r=-1\). B: \(a=4,\ r=-\frac{1}{4}\). C: \(a=0,\ r=2\).

Which have finite ordinary sums to infinity? Also find the sum for B.

options.B_only: Only B has a finite sum.
options.B_C: B and C have finite sums; A does not.

blocks.hint: A has alternating partial sums. C is the all-zero sequence, so its sum is zero.
blocks.solution:
1. A has partial sums \(4,0,4,0,\ldots\), so it does not approach one total.

  2. \[\left|-\frac{1}{4}\right|<1,\qquad S_\infty^{\mathrm B}=\frac{4}{1+\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{16}{5}.\]

  3. C has every term and every partial sum equal to zero.

blocks.html: When a question gives \(S_\infty=L\), write \(a=L(1-r)\). Combine this with the term or finite-sum condition, solve for \(r\), and check every resulting pair. Because an infinite sum is required, a nonzero candidate must also have \(|r|<1\).

blocks.title: Keep both convergent candidates
blocks.prompt: A convergent GP has \(S_\infty=20\) and \(u_2=\frac{16}{5}\). Find both possible ratios and their corresponding first terms, with the smaller ratio first.
blocks.hint: Substitute \(a=20(1-r)\) into \(ar=\frac{16}{5}\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[20r(1-r)=\frac{16}{5}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad25r^2-25r+4=0.\]
  2. \[(5r-1)(5r-4)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\frac{1}{5}\ \text{or}\ r=\frac{4}{5}.\]
  3. \[(a,r)=\left(16,\frac{1}{5}\right)\quad\text{or}\quad\left(4,\frac{4}{5}\right).\]

  4. Both ratios have magnitude less than one. Substitution verifies both original conditions.

blocks.html: A negative ratio can converge. Check its magnitude, not its sign. When rejecting a candidate, state the failed condition, such as \(|r|\ge1\).

sections.title: How much is left after the first terms?
sections.label: Signed tails and accuracy
sections.intro: For a convergent GP, the remainder \(R_n\) is the signed sum of all terms after \(u_n\). That tail is another GP, with first term \(u_{n+1}=ar^n\) and the same ratio.

blocks.html:
\[R_n=S_\infty-S_n=\frac{u_{n+1}}{1-r}=\frac{ar^n}{1-r}\quad(|r|<1).\]\[\text{Error magnitude}=|R_n|.\]

If the partial sum is above the limit, the signed remainder is negative. An error magnitude cannot be negative. For the all-zero sequence, every remainder is zero directly.

Both examples start at \(a=8\). A ratio of \(\frac13\) gives \(S_\infty=12\). A ratio of \(-\frac13\) gives \(S_\infty=6\). In the second case, \(S_3=\frac{56}{9}\) and the signed remainder \(S_\infty-S_3=-\frac29\).

With \(a=8\), a positive ratio approaches the limit from below; a negative ratio alternates around it. For \(r=-\frac{1}{3}\), the third partial sum is \(\frac{56}{9}\), so the signed gap to \(6\) is \(-\frac{2}{9}\).

To find the least number of terms for a stated accuracy, turn the required error into an inequality in \(|R_n|\). Compare consecutive integer powers, or use a calculator table, then check the proposed index and the preceding one in the original error condition. Preserve whether equality is allowed.

If \(a\ne0\) and \(0<|r|<1\), the error magnitude is multiplied by \(|r|\) at each step, so it decreases. For \(r=0\), the first term already gives the complete sum.

blocks.title: A signed remainder and a strict error bound
blocks.prompt: A GP has \(a=9\), \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\). Find the signed remainder \(R_4=S_\infty-S_4\). Then find the least positive integer \(n\) for which \(|R_n|<\frac{3}{16}\).

retry.feedback: At \(n=5\) the error equals \(\frac{3}{16}\). The question requires it to be strictly smaller.

blocks.hint: The sum to infinity is \(6\), so \(R_n=6\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\). Compare error magnitudes at consecutive indices.
blocks.solution:
1. \[R_4=6\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^4=\frac{3}{8}.\]
  2. \[|R_n|=\frac{6}{2^n}<\frac{3}{16}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad2^n>32.\]
  3. \[|R_5|=\frac{3}{16},\qquad|R_6|=\frac{3}{32}.\]

  4. The errors shrink by a factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\). Equality fails the strict bound at \(n=5\), so the least index is \(6\).

blocks.html: The tail after the first \(n\) terms begins at \(u_{n+1}\), not \(u_n\). Do not replace a signed remainder by its magnitude unless the question asks for an error size.

glossary.definition: A sequence obtained by multiplying by a fixed number at each step.
The multiplier \(r\); calculate it by division only when the preceding term is nonzero.
The finite total \(S_n\) of the first \(n\) terms.
A series whose partial sums approach one finite value.
The limiting total \(S_\infty\), when it exists.
The remaining total \(R_n=S_\infty-S_n\), which may be negative.
The nonnegative size \(|R_n|\) of the gap to the limiting total.

examples.title: Count the multiplications
examples.question: A GP has \(a=12\), \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\). Find its sixth term.
solution:
\[u_6=12\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^5.\]

The sixth term is five multiplications after the first.

\[u_6=12\left(-\frac{1}{32}\right)=-\frac{3}{8}.\]

An odd power preserves the negative sign.

The terms are \(12,-6,3,-\frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{4},-\frac{3}{8}\).

The sign alternates while the magnitude halves.

examples.title: Pair each ratio with its own first term
examples.question: A GP has \(u_2=18\) and \(u_4=8\). Find all real pairs \((a,r)\). Which pair remains if every term is positive?
solution:
\[ar=18,\qquad ar^3=8,\qquad r^2=\frac{8}{18}=\frac{4}{9}.\]

The nonzero given second term permits division.

\[r=\frac{2}{3}\quad\text{or}\quad r=-\frac{2}{3}.\]

The gap is even, so both real square roots must be considered.

\[(a,r)=\left(27,\frac{2}{3}\right)\quad\text{or}\quad\left(-27,-\frac{2}{3}\right).\]

Substitute each ratio into the original second-term equation.
The first progression begins \(27,18,12,8\); the second begins \(-27,18,-12,8\). If every term is positive, only \(\left(27,\frac{2}{3}\right)\) remains.

examples.title: A growing GP still has a finite sum
examples.question: A GP has \(a=3\), \(r=2\). Find \(u_7\) and \(S_7\).
solution:
\[u_7=3\cdot2^6=192.\]

A term uses six multiplications after the first.

\[S_7=\frac{3(2^7-1)}{2-1}=381.\]

The finite-sum formula uses the seventh power, because seven terms are included.
The ratio is greater than one, but that creates no problem for a finite total.

examples.title: Start the block at its own first term
examples.question: A GP has \(a=5\), \(r=2\). Find the sum of terms \(4\) through \(7\), inclusive.
solution:
\[N=7-4+1=4,\qquad u_4=5\cdot2^3=40.\]

The new block contains four terms and begins with forty.

\[\text{Block sum}=\frac{40(2^4-1)}{2-1}=600.\]

Use the original ratio with the block’s own first term and length.

\[S_7-S_3=635-35=600.\]

Subtracting prefixes is an independent check; the third prefix removes exactly the unwanted terms.

examples.title: Use equal-length blocks
examples.question: The first three terms of a GP sum to \(14\). The next three sum to \(112\). Find \(a\), \(r\) and \(S_6\).
solution:
\[112=r^3(14)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r^3=8\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=2.\]

Each term in the second block is three multiplications after its matching first-block term.
\[a(1+2+4)=14\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=2.\]

\[S_6=14+112=126.\]

The two supplied blocks together are the first six terms.

examples.title: Use a term condition with a finite sum
examples.question: A GP has \(u_2=6\) and \(S_3=21\). Find all possible pairs \((a,r)\).
solution:
\[ar=6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r\ne0,\qquad a=\frac{6}{r}.\]

A nonzero second term rules out a zero first term or ratio.

\[\frac{6}{r}+6+6r=21\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2r^2-5r+2=0.\]

The first three terms give a short sum equation without any exceptional denominator.
\[(2r-1)(r-2)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\frac{1}{2}\ \text{or}\ r=2.\]
\[(a,r)=\left(12,\frac{1}{2}\right)\quad\text{or}\quad(3,2).\]
The first three terms are \(12,6,3\) or \(3,6,12\), each with total \(21\). Both are valid because the question gives a finite sum.

examples.title: An alternating GP can converge
examples.question: A GP has \(a=8\), \(r=-\frac{1}{3}\). Decide whether its ordinary sum to infinity exists and find it.
solution:
\[|r|=\frac{1}{3}<1.\]

Successive terms shrink in magnitude even though their signs alternate.
The first partial sums are \(8,\frac{16}{3},\frac{56}{9},\ldots\). They lie alternately above and below \(6\), with a shrinking gap.

examples.title: Reconstruct from an infinite sum and a term
examples.question: A convergent GP has \(S_\infty=18\) and \(u_2=4\). Find all possible pairs \((a,r)\).
solution:
\[a=18(1-r),\qquad ar=4.\]

The infinite-sum condition first expresses the first term in terms of the ratio.
\[18r(1-r)=4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad9r^2-9r+2=0.\]
\[(3r-1)(3r-2)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\frac{1}{3}\ \text{or}\ r=\frac{2}{3}.\]
\[(a,r)=\left(12,\frac{1}{3}\right)\quad\text{or}\quad\left(6,\frac{2}{3}\right).\]
Both ratios satisfy \(|r|<1\), and each pair gives the stated second term and infinite sum. Keep both.

examples.title: The tail can be negative
examples.question: For \(a=8\), \(r=-\frac{1}{3}\), find \(S_3\), the signed remainder \(R_3\) and its magnitude.
solution:
\[R_3=S_\infty-S_3=6-\frac{56}{9}=-\frac{2}{9}.\]

The third partial sum is above the limit, so the remaining signed total is negative.

\[u_4=8\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^3=-\frac{8}{27},\qquad R_3=\frac{u_4}{1-r}=-\frac{2}{9}.\]

The omitted tail starts at the fourth term, not the third.

\[|R_3|=\frac{2}{9}.\]

An error magnitude is nonnegative; it differs from the signed remainder here.

examples.title: Find the first accurate enough partial sum
examples.question: A GP has \(a=5\), \(r=\frac{1}{2}\). Find the least positive integer \(n\) such that the error in using \(S_n\) for \(S_\infty\) is less than \(\frac{5}{32}\).
solution: \[S_\infty=10,\qquad |R_n|=\frac{10}{2^n}.\]

\[\frac{10}{2^n}<\frac{5}{32}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad2^n>64.\]

Multiply by positive quantities, preserving the strict inequality.

\[2^6=64,\qquad2^7=128.\]

A short table of integer powers locates the boundary; logarithms are not needed.
The error halves at each step. The sixth error is equal to the bound, so the least successful index is \(n=7\).

extraPractice.title: A shrinking alternating progression
extraPractice.prompt: The GP \(24,-12,6,\ldots\) continues. Find \(r\) and \(u_6\).
extraPractice.hint: Keep the negative sign inside the power.

extraPractice.title: An odd index gap
extraPractice.hint: The quotient of the given terms is the cube of the ratio.

extraPractice.title: Two signs, different first terms
extraPractice.prompt: A GP has \(u_2=-10\) and \(u_4=-40\). Find all real ratios and the corresponding first term for each sign.
extraPractice.hint: After finding the two ratios, use \(a=\frac{-10}{r}\) separately for each.

extraPractice.title: Finite does not mean convergent
extraPractice.hint: The finite-sum formula is valid because the ratio is not one.

extraPractice.title: A fractional block
extraPractice.prompt: A GP has \(a=81\), \(r=\frac{1}{3}\). Find the first value, number of terms and total in the block from term \(3\) through term \(6\), inclusive.
extraPractice.hint: The block is \(9,3,1,\frac{1}{3}\).

extraPractice.title: A zero block is not a denominator
extraPractice.prompt: A GP has \(a=6\), \(r=-1\). Find the sums of its first four terms and its next four terms. Can their quotient be used to recover \(r^4\)?

fields.label: Can the block sums be divided?

options.undefined: No: the previous block sum is zero.
options.one: Yes: dividing zero by zero gives one.

extraPractice.hint: The block relation still holds, but a zero denominator makes the quotient undefined.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[6-6+6-6=0.\]

  2. The next four terms have the same alternating values and also sum to zero.

  3. The relation \(0=(-1)^4\cdot0\) is true. Dividing by the first block sum would divide by zero, so that quotient cannot be used.

extraPractice.title: The infinite sum and its tail
extraPractice.prompt: A GP has \(a=15\), \(r=\frac{2}{5}\). Find \(S_\infty\) and the signed remainder \(R_4\).
extraPractice.hint: Check convergence, then use \(R_4=S_\infty r^4\).

extraPractice.title: A negative first term
extraPractice.prompt: A GP has \(a=-12\), \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\). Find \(S_\infty\), \(S_3\) and the signed remainder \(R_3\).
extraPractice.hint: The ratio magnitude determines convergence. Keep the sign of the first term in each formula.

starters.title: Two blocks can share one infinite total
starters.question:
The first two terms of a GP sum to \(15\). The next two sum to \(\frac{15}{4}\).

Find every real ratio and its corresponding first term. Show through your values that both progressions converge, and give their common sum to infinity.
starters.hint: The second two-term block equals \(r^2\) times the first. Then solve \(a(1+r)=15\) for each ratio.
starters.solution:
1. \[r^2=\frac{\frac{15}{4}}{15}=\frac{1}{4}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\pm\frac{1}{2}.\]
  2. \[r=\frac{1}{2}:\ a=10;\qquad r=-\frac{1}{2}:\ a=30.\]

  3. Both have \(|r|=\frac{1}{2}<1\), so both infinite sums exist.

  4. \[\frac{10}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=20,\qquad\frac{30}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=20.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use the equal-length block relation to obtain \(r^2=\frac{1}{4}\).
  • 1 mark: retain both ratios \(\pm\frac{1}{2}\).
  • 1 mark: pair the positive ratio with \(a=10\).
  • 1 mark: pair the negative ratio with \(a=30\).
  • 1 mark: justify convergence for both using \(|r|<1\).
  • 1 mark: calculate and confirm the common infinite sum \(20\).

starters.title: Convergence removes one algebraic candidate
starters.question: A convergent GP has \(S_\infty=8\) and \(u_2=-6\). Find its ratio, first term and fifth term.
starters.hint: Use \(a=8(1-r)\), then impose the convergence condition on every algebraic root.
starters.solution:
1. \[8r(1-r)=-6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad4r^2-4r-3=0.\]
  2. \[(2r+1)(2r-3)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=-\frac{1}{2}\ \text{or}\ r=\frac{3}{2}.\]

  3. The ratio \(\frac{3}{2}\) is inadmissible because its magnitude exceeds one. Hence \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\).

  4. \[a=8\left(1+\frac{1}{2}\right)=12,\qquad u_5=12\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^4=\frac{3}{4}.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: express the first term as \(a=8(1-r)\).
  • 1 mark: combine this with \(ar=-6\) to form the quadratic.
  • 1 mark: obtain both algebraic ratios \(-\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{3}{2}\).
  • 1 mark: reject \(\frac{3}{2}\) using the convergence condition.
  • 1 mark: obtain \(a=12\).
  • 1 mark: calculate \(u_5=\frac{3}{4}\).

starters.title: A signed tail and an inclusive accuracy target
starters.question:
A GP has \(a=18\), \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\).

Find \(S_\infty\), the signed remainder \(R_5\) and its magnitude. Then find the least positive integer \(n\) such that \(|R_n|\le\frac{3}{32}\).
starters.hint: The error magnitude is \(\frac{12}{2^n}\). Equality is permitted at the stated target.
starters.solution:
1. \[S_\infty=\frac{18}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=12.\]
  2. \[R_5=12\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^5=-\frac{3}{8},\qquad |R_5|=\frac{3}{8}.\]
  3. \[\frac{12}{2^n}\le\frac{3}{32}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad2^n\ge128.\]
  4. \[|R_6|=\frac{3}{16}>\frac{3}{32},\qquad|R_7|=\frac{3}{32}.\]

  5. The errors halve each time, so the least index is \(n=7\). Equality is sufficient here.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the convergent sum \(S_\infty=12\).
  • 1 mark: use \(R_n=12\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\).
  • 1 mark: distinguish \(R_5=-\frac{3}{8}\) from \(|R_5|=\frac{3}{8}\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the inclusive power condition \(2^n\ge128\).
  • 1 mark: check the error magnitudes at \(n=6\) and \(n=7\).
  • 1 mark: conclude that the least index is \(7\), with equality allowed.

starters.title: Recover the length, then take the last block
starters.question: A finite GP has first term \(3\), ratio \(2\), and sum \(1533\). Find its number of terms and the sum of its last three terms.
starters.hint: First find the length from the finite-sum formula. The last three terms form an inclusive block at the end.
starters.solution:
1. \[3(2^n-1)=1533\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2^n=512=2^9.\]

  2. Thus \(n=9\), and the last three terms have indices \(7,8,9\).

  3. \[u_7=192,\qquad u_8=384,\qquad u_9=768.\]
  4. \[\text{Last block sum}=192+384+768=1344.\]
  5. \[S_9-S_6=1533-189=1344.\]

    The prefix difference checks that exactly the final three terms were retained.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use the finite-sum equation \(3(2^n-1)=1533\).
  • 1 mark: isolate \(2^n=512\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the positive integer count \(n=9\).
  • 1 mark: identify the last-three-term block as indices \(7\) through \(9\), or subtract \(S_6\) from \(S_9\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the block sum \(1344\).

revision.body:
Identify the first included term, the number of terms and whether the question asks for a finite total or a limiting total.

Terms and candidates

\(u_n=ar^{n-1}\) for nonzero \(r\); \(u_1=a\). For \(r=0\), the sequence is \(a,0,0,\ldots\).

Divide known nonzero terms to obtain \(r^{j-i}\). Keep both signs after an even power, paired with their own first terms.

Finite sums and blocks

\[S_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}\quad(r\ne1).\]

For \(r=1\), use \(S_n=na\). Subtracting \(rS_n\) from \(S_n\) proves the formula.

A block is \(S_q-S_{p-1}\), with \(q-p+1\) terms. Consecutive blocks of \(k\) terms have sums differing by a factor \(r^k\); divide only by a nonzero sum.

Infinite sums

\[S_\infty=\frac{a}{1-r}\quad(|r|<1).\]

For a nonzero GP this condition is necessary. Neither \(r=1\) nor \(r=-1\) works. The all-zero sequence has sum zero for any multiplier.

Use \(a=S_\infty(1-r)\) to reconstruct a GP, then check every candidate.

Remainders and accuracy

\[R_n=\frac{u_{n+1}}{1-r}=\frac{ar^n}{1-r}\quad(|r|<1).\]

The tail starts after term \(n\). Use \(|R_n|\) for error size. Zero sequences have zero tails.

For an integer cutoff, compare consecutive powers and check neighbouring indices in the original inequality.
revision.checks:
• Term power \(n-1\), sum power \(n\)?
  • All candidate pairs checked?
  • Convergence verified before using \(S_\infty\)?
  • Signed tail or nonnegative error; strict or inclusive bound?

orig_series_trig_arithmetic.description: Translate ordered terms, angle expressions and linked sums into equations, then keep exactly the parameter values and indices that satisfy the original conditions.

sections.title: How do I test consecutive terms in their stated order?
sections.label: Order and equal differences
sections.intro: For three consecutive terms \(A,B,C\), in that order, an AP has equal adjacent differences. The middle value is the average of the two outside values:

blocks.html:
\[B-A=C-B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad2B=A+C.\]

Then \(d=B-A\). A negative or zero difference is valid unless the question imposes a restriction.

Terms in orderSuccessive differencesArithmetic?
\(7,2,-3\)\(-5,-5\)Yes
\(0,5,10,16\)\(5,5,6\)No

Equal spacing in index means equal signed changes in value. A fourth term creates a third difference that must also match.

Keep the given order. Rearranging the values changes which expression is the middle term. For four or more terms, check every adjacent difference; passing the test on only the first three is insufficient.

blocks.title: Check every adjacent difference
blocks.prompt: The expressions \(x+1,\ 2x+3,\ 3x+5,\ 5x+7\), in that order, are four consecutive terms of an AP. Find \(x\) and the common difference.
blocks.hint: The first two differences are automatically equal. The final difference supplies the remaining condition.
blocks.solution:
1. \[d_1=x+2,\qquad d_2=x+2,\qquad d_3=2x+2.\]
  2. \[x+2=2x+2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0.\]

  3. The actual terms are \(1,3,5,7\), so \(d=2\).

sections.title: Which parameter roots are actually allowed?
sections.label: Roots and extra restrictions
sections.intro: Substitute the expressions into the AP condition and solve the complete equation. Keep every real root at this stage. For each candidate, reconstruct the actual terms and calculate the common difference. Only then apply the stated restrictions.

blocks.html: “Non-constant AP” means \(d\ne0\). It does not mean that a parameter such as \(x\) is nonzero. Positive terms, a positive parameter and a positive difference are also different conditions.

blocks.title: Zero parameter does not mean zero difference
blocks.prompt: The expressions \(t^2,\ 3t+18,\ 36\), in that order, form an AP. Find every real \(t\), then retain only the values giving a non-constant AP. Give its common difference.

retry.feedback: Non-constant means \(d\ne0\), not \(t\ne0\). Reconstruct the actual terms.

blocks.hint: Factor the equation. Then substitute each root into the terms before applying the non-constant condition.
blocks.solution:
1. \[2(3t+18)=t^2+36\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t(t-6)=0.\]

  2. At \(t=0\), the terms are \(0,18,36\), with \(d=18\). At \(t=6\), they are \(36,36,36\), with \(d=0\).

  3. Only \(t=0\) gives a non-constant AP.

blocks.html: From \(x(x-4)=0\), dividing by \(x\) loses the root \(x=0\). Factor and test each branch. The same warning applies when the factor is \(\sin\theta\) or \(\cos\theta\).

sections.title: How do trigonometric terms change the method?
sections.label: Identities and complete angle sets
sections.intro: The AP rule stays the same. First write \(2B=A+C\), then use \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) to reduce the condition to one trigonometric ratio. Solve every algebraic branch and reject sine or cosine values outside \([-1,1]\).

blocks.html: A squared equation such as \(\cos^2\theta=c\) gives \(\cos\theta=\pm\sqrt{c}\) when \(0\le c\le1\). Use the signs and reference angles to find every solution in the stated interval. Check whether its endpoints are included.

For degree answers, one full turn is \(360^\circ\); for radians it is \(2\pi\). For a transformed argument, set \(\phi=2\theta\), transform the complete interval for \(\theta\) into an interval for \(\phi\), find every allowed \(\phi\), then divide each by \(2\). This uses no double-angle identity.

The positive and negative cosine levels are \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) and \(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\). On \(0^\circ\le\theta<360^\circ\), the four angles are \(30^\circ,150^\circ,210^\circ,330^\circ\).

The equation \(\cos^2\theta=\frac{3}{4}\) has four solutions in \(0^\circ\le\theta<360^\circ\), because both signs of cosine are allowed.

blocks.title: Use both signs in radians
blocks.prompt: The values \(2\sin^2\theta,\ \frac{7}{8},\ \cos^2\theta\), in that order, form an AP. Find every \(\theta\) in \(-\pi\le\theta\le\pi\), and the common difference.
blocks.hint: Replace \(\cos^2\theta\) by \(1-\sin^2\theta\). Then solve both signs of the sine value.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{7}{4}=2\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1+\sin^2\theta.\]
  2. \[\sin\theta=\pm\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\theta=-\frac{2\pi}{3},-\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{2\pi}{3}.\]
  3. \[d=\frac{7}{8}-\frac{3}{2}=-\frac{5}{8}.\]

blocks.title: Reject a ratio outside its range
blocks.prompt: The values \(\sin^2\theta,\ \sin\theta,\ 0\), in that order, form an AP, with \(0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ\). Find every permitted angle. Which of these angles gives a non-constant AP? Enter “no solutions” if none does.
blocks.hint: Factor the sine equation. A sine value greater than one is impossible.
blocks.solution:
1. \[2\sin\theta=\sin^2\theta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sin\theta(\sin\theta-2)=0.\]

  2. Reject \(\sin\theta=2\). The remaining branch \(\sin\theta=0\) gives \(0^\circ,180^\circ,360^\circ\); both endpoints are included.

  3. Each angle gives \(0,0,0\), so none gives a non-constant AP.

blocks.html: After finding the angles, return to the original terms to find \(d\). Different branches can produce different differences, especially when an unsquared sine or cosine appears.

sections.title: How do I link two different arithmetic progressions?
sections.label: Separate parameters and indices

blocks.html:
\[u_n=a+(n-1)d,\qquad v_n=b+(n-1)e.\]

Use separate first terms and differences until the question explicitly links them. A shared value may appear at different indices.

Write each progression’s sum with its own parameters too: \(S_n=\frac{n}{2}(2a+(n-1)d)\) and \(T_n=\frac{n}{2}(2b+(n-1)e)\). Translate a relation such as \(v_2=u_3\) into \(b+e=a+2d\); do not silently identify the first terms.

blocks.title: Linked observations use different indices
blocks.prompt: AP \(U\) has \(u_2=7\) and \(u_6=19\). AP \(V\) has \(v_1=u_4\) and \(v_4=u_8\). Find the first term \(b\), common difference \(e\), and sixth term of \(V\).
blocks.hint: Find the two needed values in \(U\), then place them at their stated positions in \(V\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[4d=19-7=12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=3,\qquad a=4.\]
  2. \[u_4=13,\qquad u_8=25.\]
  3. \[b=13,\qquad b+3e=25\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e=4.\]
  4. \[v_6=13+5(4)=33.\]

blocks.html: A regularly selected subsequence is another useful link. If you move \(h\) places through the original AP each time, its selected values differ by \(hd\). Find the new first term from the first selected index. For a rule \(v_n=u_{hn+k}\), substitute the whole index into the original term formula, then simplify; the chosen indices must be positive integers.

sections.title: What if the conditions are about sums or moving endpoints?
sections.label: Sums as values and index changes
sections.intro: Prefix sums are numbers and can themselves be the consecutive terms of another AP. If \(S_p,S_q,S_r\) are in that order, apply the AP condition to the totals:

blocks.html:
\[2S_q=S_p+S_r.\]

Substitute each prefix-sum formula. Do not replace the sums by individual terms or assume that the three indices are equally spaced.

Equal neighbouring prefixes have one zero added term: \(S_n=S_{n-1}\) implies \(u_n=0\). Equal non-neighbouring prefixes mean only that the intervening block totals zero; its individual terms need not be zero.

For a doubled index, the next \(n\) terms are the first \(n\) terms increased individually by \(nd\). Their sum is therefore \(S_n+n^2d\).

\[S_{2n}=2S_n+n^2d.\]

This is an identity for every positive integer \(n\), even when \(S_n=0\). No division by a sum is needed.

blocks.title: Equal neighbouring sums and a doubled index
blocks.hint: The fifth term must be zero. For the doubled index, use \(S_8=2S_4+16d\).

blocks.html: When a block endpoint depends on an unknown index, write its first index, last index and inclusive count before forming a sum equation.

\[u_n+\cdots+u_{2n}=S_{2n}-S_{n-1}\quad(n+1\text{ terms}).\]\[u_{n+1}+\cdots+u_{2n}=S_{2n}-S_n\quad(n\text{ terms}).\]

Solve for the index, then retain only positive integers that satisfy the original condition.

Let \(u_k=2k-1\). Moving the start from term \(6\) to term \(7\) removes \(u_6=11\).

StartIncluded termsCountSum
\(6\)\(11,13,15,17,19,21,23\)\(7\)\(S_{12}-S_5=144-25=119\)
\(7\)\(13,15,17,19,21,23\)\(6\)\(S_{12}-S_6=144-36=108\)

For \(n=6\), the block from term \(n\) through term \(2n\) includes seven terms. Starting at \(n+1\) instead removes the value \(11\) and leaves six terms.

blocks.title: A moving block includes its starting term
blocks.prompt: An AP has \(u_k=2k\). The sum of terms \(n\) through \(2n\), inclusive, is \(90\). Find the positive integer \(n\), the number of terms in the block and \(S_{2n}\).
blocks.hint: The block has \(n+1\) terms, with first value \(2n\) and last value \(4n\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{n+1}{2}(2n+4n)=90\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n^2+n-30=0.\]
  2. \[(n-5)(n+6)=0.\]

  3. Only \(n=5\) is a positive integer. The block contains \(6\) terms.

  4. \[S_{10}=2+4+\cdots+20=110.\]

sections.title: Can the same expressions describe an AP and a GP?
sections.label: One triple or two models?
sections.intro: Distinguish two questions: whether one fixed ordered numerical triple has both properties, and whether the same expressions can produce either type at different parameter values.

blocks.html:
Write a three-term AP as \(m-d,m,m+d\). If that same ordered triple is also a GP, its middle square must equal the product of the outside terms:

\[m^2=(m-d)(m+d)=m^2-d^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=0.\]

Thus the triple must be constant. A nonzero constant triple has ratio \(1\); the all-zero triple is generated by any multiplier.

For alternative models, solve \(2B=A+C\) for the AP and \(B^2=AC\) for the GP separately. Check each candidate in the original ordered expressions. In particular, verify that one multiplier actually takes the first value to the second and the second to the third; the squared condition alone can hide a zero-value failure.

blocks.title: Alternative models use different parameter values
blocks.prompt:
Consider the ordered expressions \(x,\ x+3,\ 2x-2\).

Find \(x\) if they form an AP. Separately, find all real \(x\) if they form a GP. Finally, choose the correct statement about one fixed ordered triple.

fields.label: One fixed triple can be both types only when…

blocks.hint: The AP and GP conditions are separate equations. For the GP candidates, check the actual consecutive ratios.
blocks.solution:
1. \[2(x+3)=x+(2x-2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=8.\]
  2. \[(x+3)^2=x(2x-2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(x-9)(x+1)=0.\]

  3. The GP triples are \(9,12,16\), with ratio \(\frac{4}{3}\), and \(-1,2,-4\), with ratio \(-2\).

  4. A single ordered triple that is both an AP and a GP must have zero common difference, so it is constant.

blocks.html: State which model each answer belongs to. Different parameter values produce different numerical triples, so separate AP and GP answers need not be equal.

glossary.definition: Three values in a stated first, middle and last position.
Adjacent terms with no skipped index.
A value that determines the terms of the progression.
An AP whose common difference satisfies \(d\ne0\).
An algebraic solution still to be checked against the original conditions.
One separate case arising from a factor or a choice of sign.
Different progressions connected by specified term or sum relations.
The total \(S_n\) of the first \(n\) terms.

examples.title: A negative parameter and a decreasing AP
examples.question: The expressions \(x+2,\ 2x-1,\ 5x+4\), in that order, are consecutive AP terms. Find \(x\) and \(d\).
solution:
\[2(2x-1)=(x+2)+(5x+4).\]

Use the expression in the middle position as the middle term.
\[4x-2=6x+6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=-4.\]

The terms are \(-2,-9,-16\). Both differences equal \(-7\), so \(d=-7\).

Negative parameter values and negative common differences are allowed unless restricted.

examples.title: Three matching terms are not enough for a four-term claim
examples.question: The expressions \(k-2,\ 2k+1,\ 3k+4,\ 5k+5\), in that order, are four consecutive terms of an AP. Find \(k\).
solution:
\[d_1=k+3,\qquad d_2=k+3,\qquad d_3=2k+1.\]

Calculate all three adjacent differences.

\[k+3=2k+1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=2.\]

The first equality holds for every parameter, but the last does not.
At \(k=2\), the terms are \(0,5,10,15\), confirming a common difference of \(5\).

examples.title: The zero parameter gives the non-constant case
examples.question: The expressions \(x^2,\ 2x+8,\ 16\), in that order, form an AP. Find all real \(x\), then determine which values remain if the AP must be non-constant.
solution:
\[2(2x+8)=x^2+16\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x(x-4)=0.\]

Factor instead of dividing by the parameter.
\[x=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=4.\]
At \(x=0\), the terms are \(0,8,16\), with \(d=8\). At \(x=4\), the terms are \(16,16,16\), with \(d=0\).
Both roots give an AP. Only \(x=0\) remains under the extra condition \(d\ne0\).

examples.title: One squared ratio gives four degree solutions
examples.question: The ordered values \(\sin^2\theta,\ \frac{7}{8},\ 2\cos^2\theta\) form an AP, where \(0^\circ\le\theta<360^\circ\). Find all angles and the common difference.
solution:
\[\frac{7}{4}=\sin^2\theta+2\cos^2\theta=1+\cos^2\theta.\]

Use the AP condition before applying the basic identity.

\[\cos^2\theta=\frac{3}{4}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\cos\theta=\pm\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\]

Taking a square root gives both signs.

\[\theta=30^\circ,150^\circ,210^\circ,330^\circ.\]

Use the reference angle and all quadrants that satisfy either sign in the stated interval.

\[d=\frac{7}{8}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{5}{8}.\]

Every solution has the same squared values, so the same difference works for all four.

examples.title: Do not divide away a trigonometric branch
examples.question: The ordered values \(\sin^2\theta,\ \frac{1}{2}\sin\theta,\ 0\) form an AP, for \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\). Find all angles and identify which gives a non-constant AP.
solution:
\[\sin\theta=\sin^2\theta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sin\theta(\sin\theta-1)=0.\]

Dividing by sine would lose every zero-sine solution.

\[\sin\theta=0:\quad\theta=0,\pi,2\pi;\qquad\sin\theta=1:\quad\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}.\]

The interval includes both endpoint angles.
At \(0,\pi,2\pi\), the terms are \(0,0,0\), with \(d=0\). At \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), they are \(1,\frac{1}{2},0\), with \(d=-\frac{1}{2}\).
All four angles satisfy the AP condition; only \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) gives a non-constant AP.

examples.title: Two APs have their own parameters
examples.question: AP \(U\) has \(u_3=8\), \(u_5=14\). AP \(V\) has \(v_2=u_3\) and a sum of \(42\) for its first four terms. Find the first terms and differences of both APs, and \(v_6\).
solution:
\[a+2d=8,\qquad a+4d=14\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=3,\ a=2.\]

Use separate symbols for the first progression.

\[b+e=8,\qquad2(2b+3e)=42.\]

The shared value is the second term of the second progression, not its first.
\[2b+2e=16,\qquad2b+3e=21\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e=5,\ b=3.\]
Here \(a\ne b\) and \(d\ne e\), even though a term value is shared.

examples.title: The new AP consists of totals
examples.question: For an AP with prefix sums \(S_n\), the values \(S_2,S_4,S_7\), in that order, form an AP. Given that \(u_3=-16\), find \(a\) and \(d\).
solution:
\[S_2=2a+d,\quad S_4=4a+6d,\quad S_7=7a+21d.\]

These are sums, so use the sum formula for each stated index.
\[2(4a+6d)=(2a+d)+(7a+21d)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=-10d.\]
\[a+2d=-16\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=2,\qquad a=-20.\]

\[S_2=-38,\qquad S_4=-68,\qquad S_7=-98.\]

The three totals really do have equal differences, each minus thirty.

examples.title: Equal adjacent prefixes reveal one zero term
examples.question: An AP has \(S_5=S_6=30\). Find \(a\), \(d\) and \(S_{10}\).
solution: \[u_6=S_6-S_5=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a+5d=0.\]
\[S_5=5a+10d=30\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a+2d=6.\]
\[3d=-6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=-2,\qquad a=10.\]

\[S_{10}=2S_5+5^2d=60-50=10.\]

The second block of five terms is lower than the first, so doubling the first sum alone would be wrong.

examples.title: Both endpoints move with the unknown index
examples.question: An AP has \(u_k=2k-1\). The sum of terms \(n\) through \(2n\), inclusive, is \(119\). Find the positive integer \(n\) and \(S_{2n}\).
solution:
\[N=n+1,\qquad u_n=2n-1,\qquad u_{2n}=4n-1.\]

Both endpoint values and the number of included terms depend on the same index.
\[3n^2+2n-120=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(n-6)(3n+20)=0.\]
Only \(n=6\) is a positive integer. The selected terms have indices \(6\) through \(12\), so there are \(7\) of them.

\[S_{12}-S_5=144-25=119.\]

Subtract the prefix before the starting term, not the prefix including it.

examples.title: The same expressions need not give the same numerical triple
examples.question: Consider the ordered expressions \(x,\ x+2,\ 2x+1\). Find \(x\) if they form an AP. Separately, find all real \(x\) if they form a GP.
solution: \[2(x+2)=x+(2x+1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=3.\]
\[(x+2)^2=x(2x+1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(x-4)(x+1)=0.\]
At \(x=4\), the GP is \(4,6,9\), with ratio \(\frac{3}{2}\). At \(x=-1\), it is \(-1,1,-1\), with ratio \(-1\).
The numerical triples are different. This does not contradict the fact that one fixed ordered triple cannot be both non-constant types.

extraPractice.title: A negative parameter with a positive difference
extraPractice.prompt: The ordered expressions \(x-3,\ 2x+1,\ 4x+8\) are consecutive AP terms. Find \(x\) and \(d\).
extraPractice.hint: Double the middle expression before simplifying.

extraPractice.title: Both roots can remain non-constant
extraPractice.prompt: The ordered expressions \(x^2,\ 3x+4,\ 8\) form a non-constant AP. Find every allowed \(x\), and give the difference for each of the two candidate values \(0\) and \(6\).
extraPractice.hint: The non-constant condition concerns the actual common difference for each reconstructed triple.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[2(3x+4)=x^2+8\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x(x-6)=0.\]

  2. At \(x=0\), the triple is \(0,4,8\), with \(d=4\). At \(x=6\), it is \(36,22,8\), with \(d=-14\).

  3. Both differences are nonzero, so both parameters remain.

extraPractice.title: The fourth term can make the conditions inconsistent
extraPractice.prompt: Find every real \(x\) for which \(x,\ 2x+1,\ 4x+2,\ 7x+4\), in that order, are consecutive AP terms. Enter “no solutions” if necessary.
extraPractice.hint: The first three terms impose one equation. Check the fourth term at the resulting value.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[2(2x+1)=x+(4x+2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0.\]

  2. At \(x=0\), the four values are \(0,1,2,4\). Their differences are \(1,1,2\), so the four-term condition fails.

  3. There is no permitted value.

extraPractice.title: A linear trigonometric condition
extraPractice.prompt: The ordered values \(\sin\theta,\ \frac{1}{4},\ 0\) form an AP, for \(0^\circ\le\theta<360^\circ\). Find all angles and the common difference.
extraPractice.hint: The AP condition gives a positive sine value, so check both relevant quadrants.

extraPractice.title: A zero angle can give a non-constant AP
extraPractice.prompt: The ordered values \(\cos^2\theta,\ \frac{1}{2}\cos\theta,\ 0\) form an AP for \(-\pi\le\theta\le\pi\). Find all angles, then the subset giving a non-constant AP.
extraPractice.hint: Factor \(\cos\theta(\cos\theta-1)=0\), then reconstruct the terms for each branch.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\cos\theta=0:\ \theta=\pm\frac{\pi}{2};\qquad\cos\theta=1:\ \theta=0.\]

  2. The zero-cosine branch gives \(0,0,0\). At \(\theta=0\), the terms are \(1,\frac{1}{2},0\), with nonzero difference \(-\frac{1}{2}\).

extraPractice.title: A new progression from selected indices
extraPractice.prompt: AP \(U\) is defined by \(u_k=2k+3\). Define \(v_n=u_{3n-1}\), for positive integer \(n\). Find the first term and common difference of \(V\), and \(v_{10}\).
extraPractice.hint: Substitute the whole original index \(3n-1\) into the rule for \(u_k\).

extraPractice.title: Prefix totals form another AP
extraPractice.prompt: For an AP, \(S_1,S_3,S_6\), in that order, form an AP. Also \(u_2=-16\). Find the original \(a\), original \(d\), and the common difference of the three selected totals.
extraPractice.hint: Use \(2S_3=S_1+S_6\), then combine it with \(a+d=-16\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[2(3a+3d)=a+(6a+15d)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=-9d.\]
  2. \[a+d=-16\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=2,\ a=-18.\]
  3. \[S_1=-18,\quad S_3=-48,\quad S_6=-78.\]

  4. The selected totals have common difference \(-30\).

extraPractice.title: Equal non-neighbouring prefixes need no zero term
extraPractice.hint: The fifth and sixth terms have sum zero; neither is individually required to be zero.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[4a+6d=24,\qquad6a+15d=24.\]
  2. \[2a+9d=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=-2,\ a=9.\]
  3. \[u_5=1,\qquad u_6=-1.\]

  4. The added block totals zero through cancellation.

starters.title: Apply positivity to the terms, not to a guessed parameter
starters.question:
The ordered expressions \(t^2,\ 4t+9,\ 18\) are the first three terms of an AP.

  1. Find all real values of \(t\).

(b) If these first three values must all be strictly positive, find the permitted \(t\), the common difference and \(S_6\).
starters.hint: The positivity condition applies to the first three terms only. Later terms may be negative.
starters.solution:
1. \[2(4t+9)=t^2+18\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t(t-8)=0.\]

  2. At \(t=0\), the terms are \(0,9,18\), so strict positivity fails. At \(t=8\), they are \(64,41,18\), all positive.

  3. \[a=64,\qquad d=41-64=-23.\]
  4. \[S_6=\frac{6}{2}(128+5(-23))=39.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the ordered AP equation.
  • 1 mark: obtain both roots \(0\) and \(8\).
  • 1 mark: reconstruct the first three values for each root.
  • 1 mark: apply strict positivity to select \(t=8\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(a=64\) and \(d=-23\).
  • 1 mark: calculate \(S_6=39\) without assuming later terms stay positive.

starters.title: Transform the complete angle interval
starters.question: The ordered values \(\sin^2(2\theta),\ \frac{5}{8},\ 2\cos^2(2\theta)\) form an AP, with \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\). Find every permitted \(\theta\) and the common difference.
starters.hint: Set \(\phi=2\theta\). Its interval is \(-\pi\le\phi<\pi\).
starters.solution:
1. \[\frac{5}{4}=\sin^2(2\theta)+2\cos^2(2\theta)=1+\cos^2(2\theta).\]
  2. \[\cos^2\phi=\frac{1}{4},\qquad-\pi\le\phi<\pi.\]
  3. \[\cos\phi=\pm\frac{1}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\phi=-\frac{2\pi}{3},-\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{2\pi}{3}.\]
  4. \[\theta=-\frac{\pi}{3},-\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3}.\]
  5. \[d=\frac{5}{8}-\frac{3}{4}=-\frac{1}{8}.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the ordered AP condition.
  • 1 mark: use the basic identity to obtain \(\cos^2(2\theta)=\frac{1}{4}\).
  • 1 mark: transform the full interval to \(-\pi\le\phi<\pi\).
  • 1 mark: include both cosine signs and all four values of \(\phi\).
  • 1 mark: divide every angle by \(2\) and retain the correct final interval.
  • 1 mark: calculate the common difference \(-\frac{1}{8}\).

starters.title: Link two progressions and then change the index
starters.question:
AP \(U\) has \(S_3=18\) and \(S_6=54\). AP \(V\) has first term \(v_1=u_4\) and common difference equal to the negative of the common difference of \(U\).

Find both first terms and both common differences. Let \(T_n\) be the sum of the first \(n\) terms of \(V\). Find the positive integer \(n\) for which \(T_n=0\), then calculate \(S_{2n}\) for \(U\).
starters.hint: Find \(U\) from its own sums first. The zero-total equation uses \(V\), but the final doubled-index sum uses \(U\).
starters.solution:
1. \[3a+3d=18,\qquad6a+15d=54.\]
  2. \[a+d=6,\quad2a+5d=18\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=2,\ a=4.\]
  3. \[b=u_4=10,\qquad e=-2.\]
  4. \[T_n=\frac{n}{2}(20-2(n-1))=n(11-n).\]

  5. The equation \(T_n=0\) has algebraic roots \(0\) and \(11\). A positive term count gives \(n=11\).

  6. \[S_{2n}=S_{22}=\frac{22}{2}(8+21\cdot2)=550.\]
starters.marking:

starters.title: Separate alternative models from a simultaneous claim
starters.question:
Consider the ordered expressions \(x,\ x+4,\ 2x+2\).

  1. Find \(x\) if they form an AP.

(b) Separately, find every real \(x\) if they form a GP.

(c) Which statement explains whether one fixed ordered numerical triple can be both a non-constant AP and a GP? Write the reasoning in your working before selecting.
starters.hint: For part (c), write an AP as \(m-d,m,m+d\) and compare the product of its outside terms with its middle square.
starters.solution:
1. \[2(x+4)=x+(2x+2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=6.\]
  2. \[(x+4)^2=x(2x+2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(x-8)(x+2)=0.\]

  3. The GP candidates give \(8,12,18\), with ratio \(\frac{3}{2}\), and \(-2,2,-2\), with ratio \(-1\).

  4. \[m^2=(m-d)(m+d)=m^2-d^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d^2=0.\]

  5. For real terms, \(d=0\), so the fixed triple is constant. The different parameter values in parts (a) and (b) produce different triples.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the AP condition.
  • 1 mark: obtain the AP parameter \(x=6\).
  • 1 mark: form the GP squared-product condition.
  • 1 mark: obtain both candidate GP parameters \(-2\) and \(8\).
  • 1 mark: check the actual common multiplier for both GP triples.
  • 1 mark: derive \(d^2=0\) for a fixed triple with both properties.
  • 1 mark: conclude that the fixed triple must be constant, distinguishing this from alternative parameter models.

revision.body:
Preserve the stated order, label what each quantity represents, and check restrictions on the reconstructed values.

Ordered terms and parameters

\[2B=A+C,\qquad d=B-A.\]

For longer lists, check every adjacent difference. Keep all real parameter roots; factor instead of dividing away zero. Non-constant means \(d\ne0\). Apply positivity to the quantities actually specified.

Trigonometric conditions

Use the AP rule, then \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\). Keep both square-root signs, reject impossible ratio values, and find all angles in the stated degree or radian interval.

Transform the interval with a transformed argument. Restore the original angle and terms; different branches can give different differences.

Linked APs and prefix relations

Use \(u_n=a+(n-1)d\) and \(v_n=b+(n-1)e\).

For totals forming an AP, use \(2S_q=S_p+S_r\). Equal adjacent prefixes give one zero term; equal separated prefixes give a zero block.

\[S_{2n}=2S_n+n^2d.\]

Moving blocks and alternative models

Terms \(n\) through \(2n\) contain \(n+1\) values and sum to \(S_{2n}-S_{n-1}\). Starting at \(n+1\) gives \(n\) values and \(S_{2n}-S_n\).

One ordered triple that is both AP and GP must be constant. Alternative parameter models use separate equations; verify the actual GP multiplier.
revision.checks:
• Order and every adjacent gap checked?
  • Zero candidates retained; \(d\ne0\) applied only when required?
  • All angle branches and endpoints checked?
  • Correct progression, prefix and inclusive indices used?
