orig_series_trig_geometric.description: Find algebraic candidates, verify a real common multiplier, and keep precisely the cases allowed by the original domain and any convergence requirement.

sections.title: When does the squared-middle test actually give a GP?
sections.label: Three checks and zero cases
sections.intro: For ordered consecutive values \(A,B,C\), a GP must have one finite real multiplier \(r\) satisfying both steps:

blocks.html:
\[B=rA,\qquad C=rB\quad\Longrightarrow\quad B^2=AC.\]

Record the original domain first. Then check the squared relation, check that a common finite multiplier really exists, and apply any extra sign, interval or convergence condition.

If \(A\ne0\), set \(r=\frac{B}{A}\) and verify \(C=rB\). This also handles \(B=0\): it gives \(r=0\) and requires \(C=0\).

If \(A=0\), the recurrence forces \(B=0\) and then \(C=0\). The all-zero triple works for every finite real multiplier, so the ratio is not unique. Every partial sum of the zero sequence is zero.

All three triples satisfy \(B^2=AC=0\). When a zero term occurs, test whether one finite multiplier actually takes each term to the next.

TripleMultiplier testResult
\(0,0,5\)The second step is impossible because \(r\cdot0\ne5\).No geometric progression
\(6,0,0\)Both steps use \(r=0\).\(S_\infty=6\)
\(0,0,0\)Every finite real multiplier works.\(S_\infty=0\)

All three triples satisfy \(B^2=AC\), but \((0,0,5)\) fails the actual multiplication rule. A zero ratio is valid for \((6,0,0)\); the all-zero triple has no unique multiplier.

blocks.title: Zero terms need the multiplier test
blocks.prompt:
Consider the ordered triples A: \((0,0,4)\), B: \((5,0,0)\), and C: \((0,0,0)\).

Which can be generated by a finite real common multiplier? Give the ratio for B, describe the multiplier for C, and give the infinite sum of the zero sequence.
blocks.hint: Check both steps \(B=rA\) and \(C=rB\). Multiplying zero by a finite number cannot produce a nonzero value.
blocks.solution:
1. A fails at the second step: \(r\cdot0\) cannot equal \(4\).

  2. B has \(r=0\): \(0=0\cdot5\) and \(0=0\cdot0\).

  3. For C, every finite real multiplier gives both zero steps. Every partial sum is zero, so its infinite sum is zero.

sections.title: How do I retain the correct parameter and sign cases?
sections.label: Paired roots and ratios
sections.intro: Use \(B^2=AC\) to generate algebraic candidates. Keep every real root, reconstruct the original values, and calculate the ratio for that same case. A positive parameter does not necessarily give a positive ratio.

blocks.html:
\[B=\pm\sqrt{AC}\qquad(AC>0).\]

If \(AC=0\), the squared equation gives just \(B=0\), followed by the zero-case checks. If \(AC<0\), there is no real middle value.

blocks.title: Pair the middle sign with the ratio sign
blocks.prompt: The ordered terms \(9,k,1\) form a GP. Find all real values of \(k\), then give the ratio when \(k\) is positive and when it is negative.
blocks.hint: The middle square is fixed, but the middle value can have either sign.
blocks.solution:
1. \[k^2=9\cdot1=9\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=\pm3.\]
  2. \[r=\frac{k}{9}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(k,r)=\left(3,\frac{1}{3}\right)\ \text{or}\ \left(-3,-\frac{1}{3}\right).\]

  3. Each pair also satisfies \(rk=1\).

blocks.html: For nonzero terms at different indices, \(\frac{u_j}{u_i}=r^{j-i}\). An odd index gap has one real ratio root; an even gap may give two signs. Match each ratio with its own first term and any stated sign restriction.
Do not combine a parameter or first term from one root with the ratio from another. A finite GP is valid even when its ratio later fails the convergence test.

sections.title: Which restrictions survive algebraic or trigonometric cancellation?
sections.label: Original domains and angle branches
sections.intro: Write every denominator restriction before simplifying. Cancelling a factor preserves equality only where the original expressions were defined. Solve the simplified equation, then return to the original terms.

blocks.title: A cancelled denominator stays excluded
blocks.prompt: The ordered expressions \(\frac{x^2-4}{x-2},\ 4,\ x+2\) form a GP. Find the roots of the simplified squared-middle equation, then the values allowed by the original expressions. Give the ratio of the permitted GP.
blocks.hint: Record \(x\ne2\) before cancelling the factor. Simplification does not remove that restriction.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}=x+2\qquad(x\ne2).\]
  2. \[16=(x+2)^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=2\ \text{or}\ x=-6.\]

  3. Reject \(x=2\), where the original first term is undefined. At \(x=-6\), the triple is \(-4,4,-4\), with \(r=-1\).

blocks.html:
\[\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\qquad(\cos\theta\ne0).\]

Use the basic identity \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) when it reduces a GP condition to one ratio. Keep all algebraic branches, reject impossible sine or cosine values, and find all angles in the stated interval.

If a square gives \(\sin^2\theta=c\) or \(\cos^2\theta=c\), consider both signs of the square root when \(0\le c\le1\). A zero factor is a separate branch. Check open and closed endpoints, all original denominators and the actual GP recurrence for every angle.

blocks.title: Two angles produce opposite ratios
blocks.prompt: The ordered expressions \(\tan\theta,\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\ \cos\theta\) form a GP, where \(0<\theta<\pi\). Find all allowed angles. Give the ratio for the acute angle and for the obtuse angle.
blocks.hint: The original tangent excludes \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\). On its domain, \(\tan\theta\cos\theta=\sin\theta\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{1}{2}=\tan\theta\cos\theta=\sin\theta.\]
  2. \[\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\quad\text{or}\quad\theta=\frac{5\pi}{6}.\]
  3. \[r=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{\tan\theta}=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}\quad\text{or}\quad-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}.\]

  4. Both original triples are defined and both recurrence steps work. These are valid finite GPs.

blocks.html: Write each angle beside its corresponding ratio. The same squared condition can give an acute case with a positive ratio and an obtuse case with a negative ratio.

sections.title: How do I find the complete convergence domain?
sections.label: Strict bounds and infinite sums

blocks.html:
\[-1<r<1,\qquad S_\infty=\frac{a}{1-r}.\]

For \(a\ne0\), the strict ratio condition is necessary and sufficient for an ordinary finite sum to infinity. Ratios \(1\) and \(-1\) fail this condition. Treat the all-zero sequence directly: its sum is zero for every finite multiplier.

If the ratio depends on a parameter, solve the full inequality and intersect it with the original domain. For \(r=\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\), with \(q(x)\ne0\), the convergence inequality is equivalent to \(p(x)^2<q(x)^2\). This avoids multiplying an inequality by a denominator whose sign is unknown.

With a non-zero first term and common ratio \(r=\frac{x-1}{x+2}\), the series converges exactly when \(-1<r<1\). This gives \(x>-\frac12\). The boundary gives \(r=-1\), and the ratio is undefined at \(x=-2\).

For an angular ratio, solve \(-1<r(\theta)<1\) within the stated degree or radian interval. On \(0<\theta<\pi\), cosine decreases from \(1\) towards \(-1\). Locate any angles where the ratio equals \(-1\) or \(1\), then test the intervals between them; exclude the strict convergence boundaries. For an integer parameter, retain only allowed integer values after solving the inequality. Neither rounding nor including a strict boundary is permitted.

blocks.title: Intersect convergence with the parameter domain
blocks.prompt:
GP X has first term \(5\) and ratio \(\frac{x+1}{x-2}\). GP Y has first term \(1\) and ratio \(2\cos\theta\), with \(0<\theta<\pi\).

Choose the complete convergence domain for each GP. Also find the infinite sum of X when \(x=-1\).

fields.label: Infinite sum of X at the stated parameter

blocks.hint: For X, compare the squares of the numerator and denominator. For Y, solve \(-\frac{1}{2}<\cos\theta<\frac{1}{2}\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[(x+1)^2<(x-2)^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad6x<3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x<\frac{1}{2}.\]

  2. This region excludes the original undefined value \(x=2\).

  3. \[-1<2\cos\theta<1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\pi}{3}<\theta<\frac{2\pi}{3}.\]

  4. Both angular boundaries give a ratio of magnitude one and are excluded.

  5. \[x=-1:\quad r=0,\qquad S_\infty=5.\]

sections.title: What changes when I select or square the terms?
sections.label: Ratio powers and derived series
sections.intro: A condition involving \(r^4\) and \(r^2\) is a quadratic in \(y=r^2\). Solve for \(y\), reject negative values, then recover every real \(r\). A positive value of \(y\) gives both signs; zero gives one ratio, \(r=0\). Apply convergence only after restoring the ratio candidates.

blocks.html:
Selecting \(u_j,u_{j+m},u_{j+2m},\ldots\) gives a GP with first term \(u_j\) and ratio \(r^m\), where \(j,m\) are positive integers.

Squaring every term gives a different GP with first term \(a^2\) and ratio \(r^2\). Use the first value actually included, and check the derived series before using an infinite-sum formula.

For nonzero derived sequences, the corresponding infinite sums are \(\frac{u_j}{1-r^m}\) and \(\frac{a^2}{1-r^2}\), with \(|r^m|<1\) and \(|r^2|<1\), respectively. A selected all-zero sequence has total zero directly.

The original progression has \(a=12\) and \(r=-\frac12\). Its first six terms are \(12,-6,3,-\frac32,\frac34,-\frac38\). Both constructions change the ratio to \(r^2=\frac14\).

ConstructionNew termsInfinite sum
Even-indexed terms\(-6,-\frac32,-\frac38,\ldots\)\(\frac{-6}{1-\frac14}=-8\)
Square each term\(144,36,9,\frac94,\ldots\)\(\frac{144}{1-\frac14}=192\)

For \(a=12\), \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\), selecting even indices starts at \(-6\), while squaring values starts at \(144\). Both new ratios equal \(\frac{1}{4}\), but their infinite sums are \(-8\) and \(192\).

blocks.title: The first included index matters
blocks.prompt:
A GP has \(a=8\), \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\). Select \(u_3,u_6,u_9,\ldots\).

Find the selected sequence’s first term, ratio and infinite sum. Separately, find \(u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2+\cdots\).
blocks.hint: The selected indices jump by three. Squaring the term values is a different operation.
blocks.solution:
1. \[u_3=8\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=2,\qquad r^3=-\frac{1}{8}.\]
  2. \[\text{Selected sum}=\frac{2}{1+\frac{1}{8}}=\frac{16}{9}.\]
  3. \[\text{Squared-term sum}=\frac{8^2}{1-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2}=\frac{256}{3}.\]

blocks.html: Summing squared terms is not the same as squaring the sum. Skipping indices also does not change the first included term into the square of the original first term.

sections.title: How do linked progressions supply the remaining equations?
sections.label: Linked GPs and AP-selected triples

blocks.html:
\[u_n=ar^{n-1},\qquad v_n=bs^{n-1}\quad(r,s\ne0).\]

Give each GP its own first term, ratio, indices and sum. For a zero ratio, use the original recurrence directly. Link only the quantities the question actually equates.

An infinite total \(L\) gives \(a=L(1-r)\) for a nonzero convergent GP. A shared term then supplies another equation. Solve every real candidate, restore its matching first term, and test both original relations and convergence.

blocks.title: Two linked sums can leave two valid pairs
blocks.prompt:
GP U has sum to infinity \(12\). GP V has sum to infinity \(8\) and ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\). Their second terms are equal.

Find both possible pairs \((a,r)\) for U, entering the smaller ratio first.
blocks.hint: V has first term \(4\), so its second term is \(2\). Use this value with U’s own infinite-sum condition.
blocks.solution:
1. \[b=8\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)=4,\qquad v_2=2.\]
  2. \[a=12(1-r),\quad ar=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad6r^2-6r+1=0.\]
  3. \[r=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{3}}{6},\qquad a=6\mp2\sqrt{3}.\]

  4. Both ratios lie between zero and one. Pair the smaller ratio with the larger first term, and check that each product \(ar\) equals \(2\).

blocks.html: If selected terms of an AP form a GP, first write each selected value as \(a+(k-1)d\) using its actual index. Apply the GP squared condition, factor, and check both recurrence steps. Keep \(d=0\) unless the AP is stated to be non-constant.

blocks.title: Keep the constant AP case until it is excluded
blocks.prompt: An AP has \(u_2=10\). Its terms \(u_1,u_2,u_4\), in that order, form a GP. Find all possible AP differences. Give the first term in the constant and non-constant cases, and the GP ratio in the non-constant case.

fields.label: First term of the constant AP
First term of the non-constant AP
GP ratio in the non-constant case

blocks.hint: Use the actual AP-indexed values \(a,a+d,a+3d\). Do not divide away the factor \(d\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[(a+d)^2=a(a+3d)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d(d-a)=0.\]

  2. If \(d=0\), then \(a=10\). If \(a=d\), the condition \(a+d=10\) gives \(a=d=5\).

  3. The selected triples are \(10,10,10\), with ratio \(1\), or \(5,10,20\), with ratio \(2\). Both are valid finite GPs.

blocks.html: An unequal selection of AP indices need not itself be an AP. The result that one ordered triple cannot be both non-constant AP and GP applies only when that selected numerical triple has both properties.

glossary.definition: One finite real number \(r\) that takes each term to the next.
The necessary relation \(B^2=AC\) for three ordered GP terms.
The values for which every original expression is defined.
A parameter or first term kept together with its corresponding ratio.
The allowed parameter values for which an ordinary finite sum to infinity exists.
Terms taken at specified indices from an original sequence.
The squares of individual term values, forming a different sequence.

examples.title: A zero middle term does not always invalidate a GP
examples.question: Decide whether \((9,0,0)\), \((0,0,9)\) and \((0,0,0)\) can be consecutive GP terms with a finite real multiplier.
solution: For \((9,0,0)\), the first step forces \(r=0\), and the second step then also works.
For \((0,0,9)\), no finite \(r\) can satisfy \(9=r\cdot0\). It is not a GP, although \(0^2=0\cdot9\).
For \((0,0,0)\), both recurrence steps work for every finite real \(r\). The multiplier is not uniquely determined.

examples.title: A positive parameter can produce alternating terms
examples.question: The ordered expressions \(4,-2x,2-x\) form a GP. Find every real \(x\) and its ratio. Which case remains if \(x>0\)?
solution: \[(-2x)^2=4(2-x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^2+x-2=0.\]
\[(x-1)(x+2)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=1\ \text{or}\ x=-2.\]
The condition \(x>0\) selects \(x=1\), even though its common ratio is negative.

examples.title: Simplifying an expression does not fill its hole
examples.question: The ordered expressions \(\frac{x^2-1}{x-1},\ 2,\ x+1\) form a GP. Find every permitted \(x\) and its ratio.
solution:
\[x\ne1,\qquad\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=x+1\quad(x\ne1).\]

Record the original denominator restriction before cancelling.
\[4=(x+1)^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=1\ \text{or}\ x=-3.\]
Reject \(x=1\), where the original first term does not exist.
At \(x=-3\), the terms are \(-2,2,-2\), and both steps use \(r=-1\).

examples.title: Cancel a trigonometric factor only on its original domain
examples.question: The ordered values \(\tan\theta,\ \frac{1}{2},\ \frac{1}{2}\cos\theta\) form a GP for \(0<\theta<\pi\). Find all angles and their corresponding ratios.
solution: The original tangent requires \(\cos\theta\ne0\), so exclude \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\).

\[\frac{1}{4}=\tan\theta\left(\frac{1}{2}\cos\theta\right)=\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta.\]

The cancellation is valid at every remaining point of the original domain.
\[\sin\theta=\frac{1}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\ \text{or}\ \theta=\frac{5\pi}{6}.\]
\[r=\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\tan\theta}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\quad\text{or}\quad-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\]
The positive ratio belongs to \(\frac{\pi}{6}\), and the negative ratio to \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\). Both original triples are defined and both recurrence steps work.

examples.title: A valid endpoint case is still excluded by an open interval
examples.question: The ordered values \(1,\ 1-\sin\theta,\ \cos^2\theta\) form a GP, with \(-\frac{\pi}{2}<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\). Find every angle and decide whether the resulting nonzero GP has an ordinary sum to infinity.
solution: \[(1-\sin\theta)^2=1-\sin^2\theta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2\sin\theta(\sin\theta-1)=0.\]
The branch \(\sin\theta=0\) gives \(\theta=0\). The branch \(\sin\theta=1\) would require \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), which is outside the open interval.
At \(\theta=0\), the triple is \(1,1,1\), with \(r=1\).
It is a valid finite GP, but its nonzero constant terms do not have an ordinary finite sum to infinity.

examples.title: Solve the full convergence domain
examples.question: A GP has first term \(3\) and ratio \(r=\frac{x-1}{x+2}\). Find all real \(x\) for which its ordinary sum to infinity exists, and express that sum in terms of \(x\).
solution: The original ratio requires \(x\ne-2\). Since the first term is nonzero, convergence requires \(|r|<1\).

\[\left|\frac{x-1}{x+2}\right|<1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(x-1)^2<(x+2)^2.\]

The denominator is nonzero, so its square is positive.
\[-2x+1<4x+4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x>-\frac{1}{2}.\]
This region lies within the original domain. The boundary \(x=-\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(r=-1\) and is excluded.
\[S_\infty=\frac{3}{1-\frac{x-1}{x+2}}=x+2\qquad\left(x>-\frac{1}{2}\right).\]

examples.title: A quadratic in the ratio squared has two sign stages
examples.question: A GP has first term \(6\) and satisfies \(4u_5-5u_3+u_1=0\). Find all real ratios, then the ratios giving an ordinary sum to infinity. Find that sum for each convergent case.
solution:
\[24r^4-30r^2+6=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad4r^4-5r^2+1=0.\]

The nonzero first term allows this simplification.
\[y=r^2\ge0,\qquad(4y-1)(y-1)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=\frac{1}{4}\ \text{or}\ y=1.\]

\[r=\pm\frac{1}{2},\quad\pm1.\]

Recover both real signs from each positive squared value.
The boundary ratios \(\pm1\) are valid finite cases but fail convergence. Keep \(r=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\).
\[r=\frac{1}{2}:\ S_\infty=12;\qquad r=-\frac{1}{2}:\ S_\infty=4.\]

examples.title: Selecting terms and squaring terms are different operations
examples.question: A GP has \(a=12\), \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\). Find the sum \(u_2+u_4+u_6+\cdots\). Separately, find \(u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2+\cdots\).
solution:
\[u_2=-6,\qquad\text{selected ratio}=r^2=\frac{1}{4}.\]

An index jump of two multiplies the original terms twice.
\[\text{squared first term}=12^2=144,\qquad\text{squared-term ratio}=r^2=\frac{1}{4}.\]
The original infinite sum is \(8\), whose square is \(64\). Squaring the total therefore does not give the sum of squared terms.

examples.title: Linked GPs keep their own first terms and ratios
examples.question: GP U has sum to infinity \(18\). GP V has sum to infinity \(16\) and ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\). Their second terms are equal. Find V’s first term and every possible pair \((a,r)\) for U.
solution:
\[b=16\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)=8,\qquad v_2=4.\]

Use the known ratio of V only in V’s equations.
\[a=18(1-r),\qquad ar=4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad9r^2-9r+2=0.\]
\[(3r-1)(3r-2)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\frac{1}{3}\ \text{or}\ r=\frac{2}{3}.\]
\[(a,r)=\left(12,\frac{1}{3}\right)\quad\text{or}\quad\left(6,\frac{2}{3}\right).\]
Both ratios satisfy \(|r|<1\), and both second terms equal V’s second term, \(4\).

examples.title: Unequal AP index gaps can produce a non-constant GP
examples.question: An AP has \(u_3=12\). The values \(u_1,u_3,u_7\), in that order, form a GP. Find every possible AP first term and difference, and the ratio of each selected GP.
solution:
\[a+2d=12,\qquad(a+2d)^2=a(a+6d).\]

Insert the actual AP indices before applying the GP condition.

\[2d(2d-a)=0.\]

Factoring keeps the possible constant-AP case.
If \(d=0\), then \(a=12\), and the selected GP is \(12,12,12\), with ratio \(1\).
If \(a=2d\), then \(4d=12\), so \(d=3\), \(a=6\). The selected GP is \(6,12,24\), with ratio \(2\).
Both are valid. The selected indices have gaps \(2\) and \(4\), so the selected triple need not itself be an AP.

extraPractice.title: A candidate can fail the definition
extraPractice.prompt: Find every real \(x\) for which \((x,0,4)\), in that order, are consecutive GP terms with a finite real multiplier. Enter “no solutions” if needed.
extraPractice.hint: The squared equation gives a candidate, but the final multiplication step still has to work.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[0^2=4x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0.\]

  2. The candidate triple is \((0,0,4)\). No finite multiplier takes zero to four, so no parameter is permitted.

extraPractice.title: A positive parameter with a negative ratio
extraPractice.prompt: The ordered terms \(9,-3x,2-x\) form a GP, and \(x>0\). Find \(x\), the ratio and the sum to infinity.
extraPractice.hint: Solve both algebraic parameter roots before applying \(x>0\).

extraPractice.title: Two finite cases at the convergence boundaries
extraPractice.prompt: The ordered expressions \(\frac{x^2-9}{x-3},\ 2,\ x+3\) form a GP. Find all permitted \(x\), and decide which corresponding GPs have ordinary finite sums to infinity.
extraPractice.hint: Keep \(x\ne3\), then check the ratios after solving the simplified equation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[4=(x+3)^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=-1\ \text{or}\ x=-5.\]

  2. Both are in the original domain. They give \(2,2,2\), with ratio \(1\), and \(-2,2,-2\), with ratio \(-1\).

  3. Both finite GPs are valid, but neither nonzero series converges.

extraPractice.title: An odd index gap fixes the angular ratio
extraPractice.prompt: A GP has ratio \(r=\sin\theta\), where \(0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\). Its terms satisfy \(u_2=3\) and \(u_5=\frac{3}{8}\). Find \(\theta\), the first term and the infinite sum.
extraPractice.hint: The index gap is three, so the quotient of the observations equals \(r^3\).

extraPractice.title: Keep a surd ratio exact
extraPractice.prompt: A GP has first term \(4\) and ratio \(\sqrt{3}-2\). Choose the correct ratio bound and find the exact sum to infinity.
extraPractice.hint: Use \(1<\sqrt{3}<2\), then rationalise the denominator if helpful.

extraPractice.title: A discrete parameter cannot sit on a strict boundary
extraPractice.prompt: A GP has first term \(2\) and ratio \(r=\frac{n-2}{3}\), where \(n\) is a positive integer. Find every \(n\) for which its ordinary infinite sum exists. Find that sum when \(n=2\).

fields.label: Infinite sum when the parameter equals two

extraPractice.hint: Solve the strict inequality first, then keep positive integers.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[-1<\frac{n-2}{3}<1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad-1<n<5.\]

  2. The positive integers are \(1,2,3,4\). The boundary \(n=5\) gives ratio \(1\) and fails.

  3. At \(n=2\), the ratio is zero, so the sequence is \(2,0,0,\ldots\), with sum \(2\).

extraPractice.title: An infinite sum determines an acute angle
extraPractice.prompt: A GP has first term \(6\), ratio \(\cos\theta\), and sum to infinity \(12\), where \(0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\). Find \(\theta\), then the sum \(u_1+u_3+u_5+\cdots\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the original infinite total to find the ratio, then select the odd indices as a new GP.

extraPractice.title: A GP at unequal AP indices
extraPractice.prompt: An AP has first term \(4\). Its terms \(u_2,u_4,u_7\), in that order, form a GP. Find all possible AP differences and the GP ratio in the non-constant AP case.

fields.label: Ratio in the non-constant AP case

extraPractice.hint: Use \(4+d,4+3d,4+6d\) as the selected terms.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(4+3d)^2=(4+d)(4+6d)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d(3d-4)=0.\]
  2. \[d=0\quad\text{or}\quad d=\frac{4}{3}.\]

  3. The non-constant case gives \(\frac{16}{3},8,12\), with ratio \(\frac{3}{2}\). The constant case also gives a valid GP.

starters.title: Keep both angular cases before applying a sign condition
starters.question:
The ordered expressions \(\tan\theta,\ 1,\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cos\theta\) form a GP, for \(0<\theta<\pi\).

Find all permitted angles and the ratio for each. Then find the sum to infinity of the case whose first term is positive.
starters.hint: The tangent excludes \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\). Find every branch before using the sign of the first term.
starters.solution:
1. \[1=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\tan\theta\cos\theta=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\sin\theta.\]
  2. \[\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\theta=\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{2\pi}{3}.\]
  3. \[r=\frac{1}{\tan\theta}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\quad\text{or}\quad-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\]

  4. Both original triples are valid and both ratios have magnitude less than one. The positive first term occurs at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}\), where \(a=\sqrt{3}\).

  5. \[S_\infty=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}}=\frac{3(\sqrt{3}+1)}{2}.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: retain the original restriction \(\cos\theta\ne0\).
  • 1 mark: derive \(\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) from the GP condition.
  • 1 mark: include both permitted angle branches.
  • 1 mark: pair each angle with its actual ratio.
  • 1 mark: verify convergence using the ratio magnitudes.
  • 1 mark: apply the positive-first-term condition to select \(a=\sqrt{3}\).
  • 1 mark: calculate the exact infinite sum \(\frac{3(\sqrt{3}+1)}{2}\).

starters.title: A ratio-squared equation and a selected series
starters.question:
A GP has first term \(8\) and satisfies \(16u_5-17u_3+u_1=0\).

Find every real algebraic ratio. The GP is then required to converge and to have a negative second term. Find the permitted ratio, the sum \(u_2+u_5+u_8+\cdots\), and the sum of all squared terms.
starters.hint: Use \(y=r^2\). The selected indices advance by three, starting at the second term.
starters.solution:
1. \[16r^4-17r^2+1=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(16y-1)(y-1)=0.\]
  2. \[r=\pm\frac{1}{4},\quad\pm1.\]

  3. Convergence removes \(\pm1\). Since \(a=8>0\), a negative second term selects \(r=-\frac{1}{4}\).

  4. \[u_2=-2,\qquad r^3=-\frac{1}{64},\qquad\text{selected sum}=\frac{-2}{1+\frac{1}{64}}=-\frac{128}{65}.\]
  5. \[\text{squared-term sum}=\frac{64}{1-\frac{1}{16}}=\frac{1024}{15}.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the quadratic in \(y=r^2\).
  • 1 mark: solve for \(y=\frac{1}{16}\) and \(y=1\).
  • 1 mark: restore all four real ratio candidates.
  • 1 mark: apply both convergence and the negative-second-term condition.
  • 1 mark: use first selected term \(-2\).
  • 1 mark: use selected ratio \(-\frac{1}{64}\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the selected infinite sum \(-\frac{128}{65}\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the squared-term sum \(\frac{1024}{15}\).

starters.title: Two infinite sums and one shared later term
starters.question:
GP U has sum to infinity \(24\). GP V has sum to infinity \(12\) and ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\). Their second terms are equal.

Find V’s first term and all possible pairs \((a,r)\) for U. Enter the smaller U ratio first.
starters.hint: V’s second term is \(3\). Use U’s own ratio in \(a=24(1-r)\), then set \(ar=3\).
starters.solution:
1. \[b=12\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)=6,\qquad v_2=3.\]
  2. \[24r(1-r)=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad8r^2-8r+1=0.\]
  3. \[r=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{2}}{4},\qquad a=6(2\mp\sqrt{2}).\]

  4. Both ratios lie strictly between zero and one. Each matched pair has product \(ar=3\) and infinite sum \(24\), so both remain.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain V’s first term \(6\) and second term \(3\).
  • 1 mark: use U’s condition \(a=24(1-r)\).
  • 1 mark: form the correct quadratic from the shared second term.
  • 1 mark: obtain both exact ratio roots.
  • 1 mark: pair each root with the correct first term.
  • 1 mark: verify both original relations and convergence, retaining both pairs.

starters.title: A geometric selection from an arithmetic progression
starters.question:
An AP has \(S_3=24\). Its terms \(u_1,u_4,u_{10}\), in that order, form a GP.

Find every possible AP difference, and the first term in each case. For the non-constant AP case, find the selected GP ratio and the original AP sum \(S_{10}\).
starters.hint: Use the actual selected values \(a,a+3d,a+9d\). Keep the zero-difference branch.
starters.solution:
1. \[a+d=8,\qquad(a+3d)^2=a(a+9d).\]
  2. \[3d(3d-a)=0.\]

  3. If \(d=0\), then \(a=8\), giving a constant selected GP. If \(a=3d\), then \(4d=8\), so \(d=2\), \(a=6\).

  4. The non-constant AP gives selected values \(6,12,24\), with ratio \(2\).

  5. \[S_{10}=\frac{10}{2}(12+9\cdot2)=150.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: insert the AP indices into the GP condition.
  • 1 mark: factor as \(3d(3d-a)=0\), retaining \(d=0\).
  • 1 mark: use \(a+d=8\) from the AP sum.
  • 1 mark: obtain the constant case \((a,d)=(8,0)\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the non-constant case \((a,d)=(6,2)\).
  • 1 mark: verify the selected multiplier \(2\).
  • 1 mark: calculate the original AP sum \(S_{10}=150\).

revision.body:
Record the original order and domain before solving. A squared equation supplies candidates; the recurrence decides whether they form a GP.

Three checks and zeros

\[B^2=AC,\qquad B=rA,\quad C=rB.\]

If \(A\ne0\), use \(r=\frac{B}{A}\), including \(r=0\). If \(A=0\), only \(B=C=0\) works; the multiplier is then nonunique and the sum is zero.

Signs and original domains

Keep every real parameter root and pair it with its own ratio. For \(y=r^2\), require \(y\ge0\), then restore both signs when \(y>0\).

Cancelled denominator restrictions remain. Keep every permitted angle branch and check endpoints, original expressions and recurrence steps.

Convergence and derived series

\[S_\infty=\frac{a}{1-r}\quad(|r|<1).\]

For \(a\ne0\), the bounds are strict. Intersect them with all original restrictions.

Selecting \(u_j,u_{j+m},\ldots\) starts at \(u_j\) with ratio \(r^m\). Squared values start at \(a^2\) with ratio \(r^2\). Check the derived series before summing.

Linked conditions

Use separate \(a,r\) and \(b,s\), with each progression’s own indices and sums. A shared term need not imply shared ratios.

For AP terms forming a GP, substitute \(a+(k-1)d\) at each selected index. Factor, retain \(d=0\) unless excluded, and verify every selected triple.
revision.checks:
• Squared condition and actual multiplier both checked?
  • Each ratio paired with the correct case?
  • Original exclusions and strict \(|r|<1\) preserved?
  • Selected first term distinguished from a squared first term?
revision.examTip: Selected first term distinguished from a squared first term?

orig_series_applications.description: Turn a stated change rule into a progression, count the exact payments or events, and test every solution against the original model.

sections.title: How do I choose a model from the words?
sections.label: Choose the rule
sections.intro: A model is a mathematical rule for the situation. First identify what changes from one step to the next. A fixed addition or subtraction gives an AP; repeated multiplication by a fixed factor gives a GP.

blocks.html:
\[\text{AP: }u_n=a+(n-1)d.\]\[\text{GP: }v_n=bq^{n-1}.\]

An increase of \(p\%\) uses \(q=1+\frac{p}{100}\). A decrease of \(p\%\) uses \(q=1-\frac{p}{100}\). In the positive-amount growth models here, the factor is positive.

Keep the first value and the index convention visible. A year-one amount \(b\) becomes \(bq^{n-1}\) in year \(n\). A lump sum \(L\) present at time zero becomes \(Lq^n\) after \(n\) complete growth periods.

Two observations may fit both an AP model and a GP model. Use the stated change rule, or an additional observation, to distinguish the proposed models. Agreement at the beginning does not make their later predictions equal.

Both sequences begin with payments of \(\pounds80\) and \(\pounds100\). Their later predictions differ.

ModelRuleThird paymentSixth payment
Arithmetic\(d=20\)\(\pounds120\)\(\pounds180\)
Geometric\(r=\frac54\)\(\pounds125\)\(\frac{15625}{64}\text{ pounds}\)

The values \(80,100\) fit both a fixed increase of \(20\) and a multiplier of \(\frac{5}{4}\). The third values are \(120\) and \(125\); by the sixth value the forecasts are \(180\) and \(\frac{15\,625}{64}\).
For a total, use the number of included terms, rather than the number of changes:

\[S_{\mathrm{AP},n}=\frac{n}{2}\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr).\]\[S_{\mathrm{GP},n}=\frac{b(q^n-1)}{q-1}\quad(q\ne1).\]

For \(q=1\), the GP is constant and its finite sum is \(nb\). A finite GP sum does not need a convergence condition.

blocks.title: Two observations can fit both models
blocks.prompt:
The first two payments are \(\text{£}\,60\) and \(\text{£}\,75\). Model A adds a fixed amount each time. Model G multiplies by a fixed positive factor.

Find the third payment under each model, to the nearest penny. Do the first two observations distinguish these two models?

fields.label: What do the two observations establish?

blocks.hint: Compare the difference \(75-60\) with the multiplier \(\frac{75}{60}\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[d=15,\qquad A_3=60+2(15)=90.\]
  2. \[q=\frac{5}{4},\qquad G_3=60\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^2=93.75.\]

  3. Both models give the observed first two payments. Their third predictions differ, so more information is needed to choose between them.

sections.title: How do I total salaries, bonuses or birthday payments?
sections.label: Receipts and inclusive indices
sections.intro: A salary stated for year one is the first term. To reach year \(n\), apply \(n-1\) increases. To total the first \(n\) salaries, include \(n\) receipts.

blocks.title: Count increases and receipts separately
blocks.prompt: A salary is \(\text{£}\,28\,600\) in year one and rises by \(\text{£}\,850\) each year. Find the salary in year six and the total salary received over the first six years. Give money answers to the nearest penny.

fields.label: Total over the first six years (£)

blocks.hint: There are five increases before the sixth salary, but six salaries in the total.

blocks.html:
For a run from year \(p\) through year \(t\), both endpoints count: there are \(t-p+1\) receipts. Find the first included value, then sum that shorter progression. For a GP it starts at \(bq^{p-1}\), with the same ratio \(q\).

The same counting works for birthdays. Payments from the twelfth through the sixteenth birthday give five payments. If a payment is made at birth, call that time zero; its age after \(k\) years is \(k\), even if it is the first payment in a list.

A total of receipts adds the payments as received. An accumulated account balance grows each payment from its own deposit date. Do not add interest to salary or birthday receipts unless the question says they are invested.
If two parts obey different rules, write two models. Add their year-specific values for a single-year payment, or add their separate sums for a multi-year total.

blocks.title: Add the two totals after modelling each part
blocks.prompt:
A worker receives a salary of \(\text{£}\,18\,000\) and a bonus of \(\text{£}\,600\) in year one. The salary rises by \(5\%\) each year; the bonus rises by \(\text{£}\,150\) each year.

Find the combined payment in year four and the combined total over the first four years, to the nearest penny. The receipts earn no additional interest.
blocks.hint: Use a GP for the salary and an AP for the bonus. Both start at index one.

blocks.html: Label your first included year or birthday, your last included one, and your count. A correct formula with the wrong first term or count models a different set of receipts.

sections.title: How long does each deposit earn interest?
sections.label: Deposit ages and valuation
sections.intro:
Mark time zero and the valuation instant before using a sum formula. Let \(P\) be each regular payment, \(L\) an optional initial lump sum, and \(q=1+i\), where \(i\) is the interest rate per period written as a decimal. Match the rate to the period length.

Use this convention: interest is credited at each period end, then any end payment is made. Value the account at time \(n\), immediately after the final interest credit and any final end payment.

blocks.html:
With \(n\) equal payments, start payments are made at times \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), so they grow for \(n,n-1,\ldots,1\) periods. End payments are made at times \(1,2,\ldots,n\), so they grow for \(n-1,n-2,\ldots,0\) periods.

\[B_{\mathrm{end}}=Lq^n+P(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1}).\]\[B_{\mathrm{start}}=Lq^n+P(q+q^2+\cdots+q^n).\]
Each bracket is a finite GP. For \(q\ne1\), summing it gives:

\[B_{\mathrm{end}}=Lq^n+P\frac{q^n-1}{q-1}.\]\[B_{\mathrm{start}}=Lq^n+Pq\frac{q^n-1}{q-1}.\]

For \(q=1\), there is no growth and both balances equal \(L+nP\). Use this directly instead of a formula with a zero denominator.

Three payments of \(\pounds400\) grow by the factor \(q=1.03\) each period. Value them just after the third interest credit and the payment due at that time.

TimingValues at third creditTotal
Start of each period\(400q^3,400q^2,400q\)\(\pounds1273.4508\)
End of each period\(400q^2,400q,400\)\(\pounds1236.36\)

Round only after adding the three values. Start-of-period payments give \(\pounds1273.45\) to the nearest penny.

At the same valuation date, three \(\text{£}\,400\) start payments have ages \(3,2,1\); three end payments have ages \(2,1,0\). At \(3\%\), their final balances are \(\text{£}\,1\,273.45\) and \(\text{£}\,1\,236.36\).

blocks.title: The same payments have different ages
blocks.prompt:
An account starts empty. A payment of \(\text{£}\,300\) is made once in each of three years. Interest of \(4\%\) is credited at each year end.

Find the balance at the end of year three for payments made at each year end, immediately after interest, and for payments made at each year start. In both cases value the account after the last interest credit and any end payment. Give both balances to the nearest penny.
blocks.hint: End payments have ages \(2,1,0\) years. Start payments have ages \(3,2,1\) years.
blocks.solution:
1. \[B_{\mathrm{end}}=300(1.04^2+1.04+1)=936.48.\]
  2. \[B_{\mathrm{start}}=300(1.04^3+1.04^2+1.04)=973.9392.\]

  3. The balances are \(\text{£}\,936.48\) and \(\text{£}\,973.94\). Only the final answers have been rounded.

blocks.html:
An initial lump sum is present from time zero in both plans and grows for the same \(n\) periods. Only the regular-payment portions differ by one extra factor of \(q\):

\[B_{\mathrm{start}}-Lq^n=q\bigl(B_{\mathrm{end}}-Lq^n\bigr).\]

With no initial lump sum, this reduces to \(B_{\mathrm{start}}=qB_{\mathrm{end}}\). With a nonzero lump sum and a nonzero interest rate, multiplying the whole end balance by \(q\) would grow that initial money for an extra period incorrectly.

The total cash paid in is \(L+nP\). If there are no other transactions, interest earned is the final balance minus this total.

blocks.title: Include the initial balance once
blocks.prompt:
An account receives \(\text{£}\,800\) at time zero and \(\text{£}\,150\) at each of the next three year ends, immediately after that year’s interest is credited.

Find its balance just after the third end payment if the annual interest rate is \(2.5\%\). Find the balance for the same payments if there is no interest. Give both answers to the nearest penny.
blocks.hint: The initial amount grows for three years. The regular payments grow for two, one and zero years.

blocks.html: Read “before” and “after” literally. Just before a scheduled end payment, leave that payment out of the balance. Keep all powers and intermediate amounts unrounded; round money only at the requested final step.

sections.title: Which parts of a bouncing path have happened?
sections.label: Bounce events and distance
sections.intro: Suppose a ball falls from height \(H>0\), and every rebound reaches a fraction \(r\) of the previous height, with \(0<r<1\). The rebound peaks are \(Hr,Hr^2,Hr^3,\ldots\). These are heights; total distance must also count the downward journeys.

blocks.html: The initial fall contributes \(H\) once. Each completed rebound of height \(h\) contributes \(2h\), one rise and one fall. At a rebound peak, the current rise has happened but its fall has not.

The symbol \(\sum\) means “add the indicated terms”. For a positive integer \(m\),

\[\sum_{k=1}^{m}Hr^k=Hr+Hr^2+\cdots+Hr^m.\]

Include one term for each integer \(k\) from \(1\) through \(m\).

Count the initial landing as ground impact one. At ground impact \(n\), exactly \(n-1\) rebounds have been completed:

\[D_{\mathrm{impact}\,n}=H+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}Hr^k.\]

The sum is empty at \(n=1\), so the first impact distance is just \(H\). After \(m\) complete rises and falls, use \(H+2\sum_{k=1}^{m}Hr^k\). At the peak of rebound \(m\), use:

\[D_{\mathrm{peak}\,m}=H+2\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}Hr^k+Hr^m.\]

1. For a drop of \(5\,\mathrm m\) followed by rebounds of ratio \(\frac35\), count the initial fall once and each complete rebound twice.
  2. At impact \(3\), the distance is \(5+2\left(3+\frac95\right)=\frac{73}{5}\,\mathrm m\). Then the upward leg to peak \(3\) adds \(\frac{27}{25}\,\mathrm m\), giving \(\frac{392}{25}\,\mathrm m\).
  3. The limiting distance is \(5+\frac{2(3)}{1-\frac35}=20\,\mathrm m\).

With \(H=5\text{ m}\) and \(r=\frac{3}{5}\), impact three occurs after two complete rebounds. The peak of rebound three adds only the upward distance \(\frac{27}{25}\text{ m}\). Horizontal spacing shows event order, not elapsed time.
For the idealised infinite model, the rebound heights form a convergent GP. Count the entire vertical path:

\[D_\infty=H+2\frac{Hr}{1-r}\qquad(H>0,\ 0<r<1).\]

This is the limiting distance predicted by the repeated-ratio model. Each finite stage leaves a positive distance still to come; the limit is not reached after a finite number of nonzero rebounds.

blocks.title: Name the exact bounce event
blocks.prompt:
A ball is released from \(4\text{ m}\). Each rebound reaches half the height of the previous fall. The initial landing is ground impact one.

Find the total vertical distance travelled by ground impact three, at the peak of rebound three, and in the idealised infinite model. Give exact values.

fields.label: Distance at the peak of rebound three (m)

blocks.hint: By impact three, the first two rebounds are complete. To reach the next peak, add just the next upward distance.

blocks.html: Write the stopping event in words before summing: impact, peak, or completed rebound. That sentence determines the last included term and whether it is counted once or twice.

sections.title: How do I find an accumulation limit or the first index near it?
sections.label: Accumulation and least indices
sections.intro: Some situations add an increment once at each event. A peg’s depth increases, for example, are added once each. There is no return journey to double. Let the first positive increment be \(c\), with ratio \(0<r<1\).

blocks.html:
\[D_n=\frac{c(1-r^n)}{1-r},\qquad D_\infty=\frac{c}{1-r}.\]\[R_n=D_\infty-D_n=\frac{cr^n}{1-r}.\]

Every increment is positive, so the accumulated total increases towards its limit. The positive remaining gap is multiplied by \(r\) at each step and therefore strictly decreases.

To find the least integer index satisfying a strict gap bound, write the inequality for \(R_n\), then test integer powers using a calculator table or repeated multiplication. Check the first successful index and the one immediately before it. The decreasing-gap property proves that every earlier index also fails.

If observations are separated by several impacts, use their actual index gap. For example, the third increment divided by the first is \(r^2\). Algebra may produce both signs; a model of positive depth increases requires a positive ratio.

blocks.title: A decreasing gap gives a least integer
blocks.prompt:
Successive impacts drive a peg farther into a surface. The first depth increase is \(1.2\text{ cm}\), and each later increase is half the previous one. Each increase is counted once.

Find the limiting depth, the depth after four impacts, and the least number of impacts for the remaining gap to the limit to be strictly less than \(0.1\text{ cm}\). Give exact depth values.
blocks.hint: The depth is a GP sum. Subtract it from the infinite sum to obtain the remaining gap, then test neighbouring integer indices.
blocks.solution:
1. \[D_\infty=\frac{\frac{6}{5}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{12}{5}\text{ cm}.\]
  2. \[D_4=\frac{12}{5}\left(1-\frac{1}{16}\right)=\frac{9}{4}\text{ cm}.\]
  3. \[R_n=\frac{12}{5}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n<\frac{1}{10}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad2^n>24.\]

  4. At \(n=4\), the gap is \(0.15\text{ cm}\); at \(n=5\), it is \(0.075\text{ cm}\). The gap decreases at every impact, so the least index is \(5\).

blocks.html: “Strictly less than” excludes equality. A question about one increment, the accumulated total, or the remaining gap uses a different expression for each. Name the requested quantity before testing an index.

sections.title: How do I connect different progressions and reject false candidates?
sections.label: Linked equations and validity
sections.intro:
Give each progression its own parameters: an AP may use \(a,d\), while a GP uses \(b,r\). Translate each stated equality using the actual term indices or sums. Sharing one term or one total does not make the first terms or change rules equal.

If a selected GP uses \(v_j,v_{j+m},v_{j+2m},\ldots\), its first included value is \(br^{j-1}\) and its ratio is \(r^m\). Check convergence of the selected series before using its infinite-sum formula.

blocks.html: For a nonzero GP, an ordinary sum to infinity exists precisely when \(|r|<1\), and then \(S_\infty=\frac{b}{1-r}\). A zero sequence has sum zero directly. A convergent alternating GP is allowed in an algebraic linked-progression question, even though positive physical increments need a positive ratio.

If expressions must form a GP, first use the ordered condition \(B^2=AC\), then verify a finite common multiplier in both steps \(B=rA\), \(C=rB\). If \(A\ne0\), use \(r=\frac{B}{A}\). If \(A=0\), only the all-zero triple works. An AP first term, a changed GP first term and their respective sums remain separate quantities.

Record restrictions before solving: real square roots, nonzero denominators, positive amounts, integer counts and convergence. Factoring can produce several cases; keep each until the original question excludes it.

Squaring preserves a valid equality but can introduce extra roots. In particular, \(\sqrt{x}\) is nonnegative. Test every candidate in the original unsquared equation, even if it is real and positive.

blocks.title: Positive algebraic roots still need the original equation
blocks.prompt:
Let \(x>0\). An AP begins with \(x-13,1\). A GP has first term \(\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2}\) and ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\). The sum of the first two AP terms equals the GP sum to infinity.

Find all roots produced by squaring the resulting equation, then all values that actually satisfy the original condition. Find the common sum in the valid case.

fields.label: Common sum in the valid case

blocks.hint: The original equation is \(x-12=\sqrt{x}\). Its right side is nonnegative.
blocks.solution:
1. \[S_{\mathrm{AP},2}=x-12,\qquad S_{\mathrm{GP},\infty}=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=\sqrt{x}.\]
  2. \[(x-12)^2=x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(x-9)(x-16)=0.\]

  3. At \(x=9\), the original sides are \(-3\) and \(3\), so reject it. At \(x=16\), both sides are \(4\), so it is valid.

blocks.html: Finish by reconstructing the quantities named in the question. Show the term or sum equality, the sign and integer checks, and the convergence check when an infinite sum is used. A calculator root alone does not establish a valid model.

glossary.definition: A mathematical rule chosen to represent the stated situation.
The factor applied once per growth or decay period.
One payment received; its amount is separate from any later interest.
The value of money after growth up to a specified date.
The exact time at which a balance is measured, including whether a payment has happened.
A one-off amount already present at time zero, separate from regular payments.
The top of a bounce, reached after the rise but before the corresponding fall.
The difference between a limiting total and the total accumulated so far.
A root introduced by an algebraic step that fails the original equation.

examples.title: The same first two values do not determine the rule
examples.question:
The first two payments are \(\text{£}\,80\) and \(\text{£}\,100\). Model A increases each payment by a fixed amount. Model G increases it by a fixed percentage.

Find the third payment and the total of the first four payments under each model.
solution: \[\text{Model G: }q=\frac{100}{80}=\frac{5}{4}.\]

The third payments are \(\text{£}\,120\) and \(\text{£}\,125\); the totals are \(\text{£}\,440\) and \(\text{£}\,461.25\). Both models fit the first two observations, but their later predictions differ.

examples.title: The fifth salary follows four increases
examples.question: A salary starts at \(\text{£}\,27\,000\) in year one and rises by \(\text{£}\,1\,200\) each year. Find the year-five salary and the total received during the first five years.
solution:
The year-five salary is \(\text{£}\,31\,800\), and the total of the five annual receipts is \(\text{£}\,147\,000\).

The number of increases is one less than the number of included annual salaries.

examples.title: A salary multiplier and a bonus increment
examples.question:
In year one, a salary is \(\text{£}\,25\,000\) and a bonus is \(\text{£}\,1\,000\). The salary rises by \(4\%\) each year, while the bonus rises by \(\text{£}\,200\) each year.

Find the combined year-four payment and the combined total for the first four years, to the nearest penny. No additional interest is earned on the receipts.
solution: The combined year-four payment is \(\text{£}\,29\,721.60\).
The combined total is \(\text{£}\,111\,361.60\). Adding a GP amount to an AP amount does not usually produce a single AP or GP; sum the components separately.

examples.title: Three deposits valued on the same date
examples.question:
An empty account receives \(\text{£}\,400\) once in each of three years. Annual interest is \(3\%\), credited at each year end.

Compare payments at the start of each year with payments at the end of each year immediately after interest. Value both accounts at the end of year three, after its interest credit and any end payment. Round the final balances to the nearest penny.
solution: Start payments earn interest for \(3,2,1\) years. End payments earn it for \(2,1,0\) years.

The final balances are \(\text{£}\,1\,273.45\) and \(\text{£}\,1\,236.36\). Each start payment has earned exactly one more year of interest, so its accumulated payment total is multiplied by \(1.03\).

examples.title: An initial lump sum has its own age
examples.question:
An account receives \(\text{£}\,1\,000\) at time zero, then \(\text{£}\,250\) at each of the next four year ends immediately after interest. Annual interest is \(2\%\).

Find the balance just after the fourth end payment, to the nearest penny.
solution: The initial sum earns four years of interest. The four regular deposits earn \(3,2,1,0\) years.
The required balance is \(\text{£}\,2\,112.83\). The original \(\text{£}\,1\,000\) is included once, separately from the four equal payments.

examples.title: Ground impact and rebound peak are different stopping points
examples.question:
A ball is released from \(5\text{ m}\). Each rebound reaches \(\frac{3}{5}\) of the previous height. Count the initial landing as ground impact one.

Find the distance travelled by impact three and then at the peak of rebound three.
solution: At impact three, two rebounds have risen and fallen completely.
\[D_{\mathrm{impact}\,3}=5+2\left(3+\frac{9}{5}\right)=\frac{73}{5}\text{ m}.\]
The third rebound peak comes next. Add its upward distance only.

examples.title: A limiting distance can determine the rebound ratio
examples.question: A ball is released from \(4\text{ m}\). Each rebound reaches a fixed fraction \(r\) of the previous height, where \(0<r<1\). Its total vertical distance in the idealised infinite model is \(28\text{ m}\). Find \(r\).
solution:
\[28=4+2\frac{4r}{1-r}.\]

Count the initial fall once and every complete rebound twice.
\[24(1-r)=8r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\frac{3}{4}.\]
This ratio is positive and less than one. Substituting it into the original distance formula gives \(28\text{ m}\), so the model is valid.

examples.title: Repeated impacts add depth once, not twice
examples.question:
A peg moves \(0.8\text{ cm}\) farther into a surface on the first impact. Each later depth increase is \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the previous increase.

Find the limiting depth and the least number of impacts needed for the remaining gap to the limit to be strictly less than \(0.2\text{ cm}\).
solution: \[D_n=\frac{\frac{4}{5}\left(1-\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^n\right)}{1-\frac{3}{4}}=\frac{16}{5}\left(1-\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^n\right).\]
\[D_\infty=\frac{16}{5}\text{ cm},\qquad R_n=\frac{16}{5}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^n.\]
\[R_n<\frac{1}{5}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^n<\frac{1}{16}.\]

Each new gap is \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the previous one. The gaps strictly decrease, so the least number of impacts is \(10\).

A table of integer powers finds the candidate; the neighbouring check and decreasing gap establish that it is the first.

examples.title: A finite AP can equal a selected infinite GP sum
examples.question:
An AP has first term \(2\) and difference \(1\). A separate GP has first term \(-21\) and ratio \(-\frac{1}{2}\).

The sum of the first \(n\) AP terms equals the sum of the even-indexed GP terms \(v_2+v_4+v_6+\cdots\). Find the positive integer \(n\).
solution: \[v_2=\frac{21}{2},\qquad\text{selected ratio}=\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{4}.\]
\[\frac{n(n+3)}{2}=14\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(n-4)(n+7)=0.\]
The index must be a positive integer, so \(n=4\). The AP sum \(2+3+4+5=14\) checks the original equality.

examples.title: Squaring can introduce a false positive candidate
examples.question: Let \(x>0\). An AP starts with \(x-3,1\). A GP has first term \(\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2}\) and ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\). The first two AP terms have the same sum as the infinite GP. Find every valid \(x\).
solution: The original right side is nonnegative, so any valid case must also have \(x-2\ge0\).
\[(x-2)^2=x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^2-5x+4=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=1\ \text{or}\ x=4.\]
At \(x=1\), the original sides are \(-1\) and \(1\), so reject it. At \(x=4\), both sides are \(2\), so it works.
The valid AP begins \(1,1\), and the GP has first term \(1\), ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\), and infinite sum \(2\). A constant AP is allowed here.

extraPractice.title: Sum only the stated run of annual receipts
extraPractice.prompt:
A grant pays \(\text{£}\,1\,200\) in year one. The annual payment rises by \(5\%\) each year.

Find the payment in year six and the total paid from year three through year six inclusive, to the nearest penny. These are receipts; no additional interest is earned on them.

fields.label: Total from year three through year six (£)

extraPractice.hint: The run starts at the third payment and contains four payments.

extraPractice.title: Birthday endpoints both count
extraPractice.prompt:
A child receives a payment on every birthday from the twelfth through the sixteenth, inclusive. Plan A starts at \(\text{£}\,40\) and increases each payment by \(\text{£}\,10\). Plan G starts at \(\text{£}\,40\) and increases each payment by \(25\%\).

Find the number of payments and the total received under each plan. Give money totals to the nearest penny. The payments are not invested.
extraPractice.hint: Label the twelfth birthday as the first included payment. The sixteenth is the fifth.

extraPractice.title: Just before the final payment
extraPractice.prompt:
An account starts empty and is scheduled to receive \(\text{£}\,200\) at each of four year ends, immediately after that year’s \(3\%\) interest credit.

Value the account at the end of year four after interest has been credited but just before the fourth payment is made. How many payments are included, and what is the balance to the nearest penny?
extraPractice.hint: The first three payments have earned three, two and one years of interest. The fourth is not in the account yet.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[B=200(1.03^3+1.03^2+1.03)=636.7254.\]

  2. Three payments are included. The balance is \(\text{£}\,636.73\).

extraPractice.title: One period with an initial lump sum
extraPractice.prompt:
An account has an initial \(\text{£}\,500\) at time zero. One extra payment of \(\text{£}\,100\) is made either at the start of the year or at the end, immediately after annual interest of \(10\%\) is credited.

Find both balances at the end of that year, after interest and any end payment, to the nearest penny. Which part receives one extra growth factor when the payment moves to the start?

options.whole: The whole account, including the initial lump sum.

extraPractice.hint: The initial amount earns one year of interest in both plans.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[B_{\mathrm{start}}=500(1.1)+100(1.1)=660.\]
  2. \[B_{\mathrm{end}}=500(1.1)+100=650.\]

  3. Only the payment portion grows for an extra year. Multiplying the entire end balance by \(1.1\) would give \(715\), which incorrectly adds another year to the original money.

extraPractice.title: Four impacts include three complete rebounds
extraPractice.prompt:
A ball is released from \(6\text{ m}\), and each rebound reaches \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the previous height. Count the initial landing as impact one.

Find the exact total distance by impact four and the limiting distance in the idealised infinite model.
extraPractice.hint: By impact four, rebound heights \(4,\frac{8}{3},\frac{16}{9}\) have each been travelled upward and downward.

extraPractice.title: Use the gap between observations
extraPractice.prompt:
Successive positive depth increases follow a GP. The first increase is \(0.5\text{ cm}\) and the third is \(0.18\text{ cm}\).

Find the physically valid ratio, the total increase after three impacts, and the limiting total increase. Give exact values.
extraPractice.hint: There are two multiplication steps from the first increase to the third. The context requires positive increases at every impact.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[r^2=\frac{0.18}{0.5}=\frac{9}{25}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\pm\frac{3}{5}.\]

  2. The negative ratio would give a negative second increase, so keep \(r=\frac{3}{5}\).

  3. \[D_3=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{10}+\frac{9}{50}=\frac{49}{50}\text{ cm}.\]
  4. \[D_\infty=\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{1-\frac{3}{5}}=\frac{5}{4}\text{ cm}.\]

extraPractice.title: A changed expression creates a different progression
extraPractice.prompt:
An AP begins \(x,x+4,x+8\). Replacing the third expression by \(x+12\) gives the first three terms of a GP with nonzero terms.

Find \(x\), the GP ratio, and the sum of the first four terms of each progression.
extraPractice.hint: Apply the squared-middle condition to the changed triple, then verify its multiplier. The original AP still has difference four.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(x+4)^2=x(x+12)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad16=4x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=4.\]

  2. The AP begins \(4,8,12\), with difference \(4\). The changed GP begins \(4,8,16\), with ratio \(2\), so its two multiplication steps agree.

  3. \[S_{\mathrm{AP},4}=\frac{4}{2}(4+16)=40,\qquad S_{\mathrm{GP},4}=4+8+16+32=60.\]

extraPractice.title: A finite sum and an alternating infinite sum
extraPractice.prompt:
An AP has first term \(1\) and common difference \(2\). A separate GP has first term \(54\) and ratio \(-\frac{1}{2}\).

Find the GP sum to infinity and the positive integer \(n\) for which the sum of the first \(n\) AP terms equals it.
extraPractice.hint: The GP converges despite alternating signs. Simplify the AP sum before solving for its index.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\left|-\frac{1}{2}\right|<1,\qquad S_{\mathrm{GP},\infty}=\frac{54}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=36.\]
  2. \[S_{\mathrm{AP},n}=\frac{n}{2}\bigl(2+2(n-1)\bigr)=n^2.\]
  3. \[n^2=36\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=6\ \text{or}\ n=-6.\]

  4. Only \(n=6\) is a positive integer index. Its AP sum is \(36\), as required.

starters.title: Two separated observations support two growth rules
starters.question:
An annual payment is \(\text{£}\,100\) in year one and \(\text{£}\,144\) in year three. Model A uses a fixed annual addition. Model G uses a fixed positive percentage increase.

For each model, find the year-two payment and the total of the first five payments, to the nearest penny. A separate record then shows the year-two payment was \(\text{£}\,122\). Which of the two proposed models agrees with this additional observation?
starters.hint: The observations are two annual changes apart. For the GP, the required factor is positive.
starters.solution:
1. \[100+2d=144\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=22,\qquad A_2=122.\]
  2. \[100q^2=144\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q=\frac{6}{5},\qquad G_2=120.\]
  3. \[S_{A,5}=\frac{5}{2}(100+188)=720.\]
  4. \[S_{G,5}=100\frac{1.2^5-1}{0.2}=744.16.\]

  5. Both models fit the year-one and year-three observations. Only Model A also predicts the recorded year-two payment of \(\text{£}\,122\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use the two-year gap to obtain \(d=22\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the positive multiplier \(q=\frac{6}{5}\).
  • 1 mark: calculate the two year-two predictions, \(122\) and \(120\).
  • 1 mark: calculate the AP total \(720\).
  • 1 mark: calculate the GP total \(744.16\).
  • 1 mark: select Model A using the additional observation, while recognising that both fit the original observations.

starters.title: Compare deposit timing without moving the initial money
starters.question:
Two accounts each receive an initial \(\text{£}\,900\) at time zero and four equal regular payments of \(\text{£}\,250\). Annual interest is \(2.5\%\), credited at each year end. No other transactions occur.

In Account S, regular payments are made at the start of each of four years. In Account E, they are made at each year end immediately after interest. Value both accounts at the end of year four, after interest and any final end payment.

Find both balances and the interest earned by Account S, all to the nearest penny.
starters.hint: Both accounts include \(900(1.025)^4\). Only the regular payments change their ages.
starters.solution:
1. Account S payments have ages \(4,3,2,1\) years; Account E payments have ages \(3,2,1,0\) years.

  2. \[B_S=900(1.025)^4+250\frac{1.025(1.025^4-1)}{0.025}.\]
  3. \[B_S=2\,057.51373046875.\]
  4. \[B_E=900(1.025)^4+250\frac{1.025^4-1}{0.025}=2\,031.5605078125.\]
  5. \[\text{Total paid}=900+4(250)=1\,900.\]
  6. \[\text{Interest in S}=B_S-1\,900=157.51373046875.\]

  7. The balances are \(\text{£}\,2\,057.51\) and \(\text{£}\,2\,031.56\); Account S earns \(\text{£}\,157.51\) interest. The initial money has the same age in both accounts.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: assign start-payment exponents \(4,3,2,1\).
  • 1 mark: assign end-payment exponents \(3,2,1,0\).
  • 1 mark: include the common initial contribution \(900(1.025)^4\) once in each account.
  • 1 mark: form the correct start-payment GP sum.
  • 1 mark: form the correct end-payment GP sum.
  • 1 mark: calculate both balances with rounding only at the final step.
  • 1 mark: subtract the total paid, \(1\,900\), to obtain the interest \(\text{£}\,157.51\).

starters.title: Infer the impact ratio and locate the first successful count
starters.question:
Each impact drives a peg farther into a surface. Its successive positive depth increases form a GP. The first increase is \(0.9\text{ cm}\) and the third is \(0.4\text{ cm}\).

Find the valid common ratio and the limiting total depth. Then find the least number of impacts for the remaining gap to the limit to be strictly less than \(0.1\text{ cm}\). Give the ratio and limiting depth exactly.
starters.hint: The first and third increases are two multiplication steps apart. After finding the positive ratio, form the gap to the limiting GP sum.
starters.solution:
1. \[0.9r^2=0.4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r^2=\frac{4}{9}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\pm\frac{2}{3}.\]

  2. Positive increases require \(r=\frac{2}{3}\). This ratio also satisfies convergence.

  3. \[D_\infty=\frac{\frac{9}{10}}{1-\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{27}{10}\text{ cm}.\]
  4. \[R_n=\frac{27}{10}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n<\frac{1}{10}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n<\frac{1}{27}.\]
  5. \[R_8=\frac{128}{1\,215}>\frac{1}{10},\qquad R_9=\frac{256}{3\,645}<\frac{1}{10}.\]

  6. The gaps strictly decrease, so \(n=9\) is the least successful integer count.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use the index gap to form \(0.9r^2=0.4\).
  • 1 mark: solve the squared ratio and select \(r=\frac{2}{3}\) from the positive-increment condition.
  • 1 mark: check convergence and calculate the limit \(\frac{27}{10}\text{ cm}\).
  • 1 mark: form the correct remaining-gap expression.
  • 1 mark: preserve the strict bound and show that the eighth gap fails it.
  • 1 mark: show that the ninth gap satisfies it.
  • 1 mark: use the decreasing gap to justify that \(9\) is the least count.

starters.title: A surd ratio and an extraneous positive parameter
starters.question:
Let \(x>0\). An AP starts with \(x-7,1\). A GP has first term \((2-\sqrt{2})\sqrt{x}\) and common ratio \(\sqrt{2}-1\). The sum of the first two AP terms equals the GP sum to infinity.

Find all parameter roots produced by squaring the resulting equation, and then all valid values of \(x\). For the valid case, find the GP first term and the common sum exactly.
starters.hint: Check the surd ratio’s magnitude, simplify the infinite sum, and compare each squared-equation candidate with the original unsquared equality.
starters.solution:
1. Since \(1<\sqrt{2}<2\), the ratio satisfies \(0<\sqrt{2}-1<1\), so the GP converges.

  2. \[S_{\mathrm{GP},\infty}=\frac{(2-\sqrt{2})\sqrt{x}}{1-(\sqrt{2}-1)}=\sqrt{x}.\]
  3. \[x-6=\sqrt{x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(x-6)^2=x.\]
  4. \[x^2-13x+36=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(x-4)(x-9)=0.\]

  5. At \(x=4\), the original sides are \(-2\) and \(2\), so reject it. At \(x=9\), both sides are \(3\), so it is valid.

  6. \[b=3(2-\sqrt{2})=6-3\sqrt{2},\qquad S=3.\]

  7. The valid AP starts \(2,1\), with difference \(-1\). Its first-two-term sum checks the common value.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: establish \(0<\sqrt{2}-1<1\).
  • 1 mark: simplify the GP infinite sum to \(\sqrt{x}\).
  • 1 mark: form the original equation \(x-6=\sqrt{x}\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the squared quadratic and both candidates \(4,9\).
  • 1 mark: reject \(x=4\) using the original equation.
  • 1 mark: verify and retain \(x=9\).
  • 1 mark: calculate the GP first term \(6-3\sqrt{2}\).
  • 1 mark: calculate and check the common sum \(3\).

revision.body:
Match the rule, terms and stopping event.

Choose and index the model

\[u_n=a+(n-1)d,\quad S_n=\frac{n}{2}\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr).\]\[v_n=bq^{n-1},\quad T_n=\frac{b(q^n-1)}{q-1}\ (q\ne1).\]

Fixed addition: AP; fixed percentage: GP. Time-zero lump at \(n\): \(Lq^n\). Include endpoints; sum components separately.

Use one valuation instant

After period \(n\)’s interest and any end payment: ages \(n,\ldots,1\) (start), \(n-1,\ldots,0\) (end).

\[F=\frac{q^n-1}{q-1}\quad(q\ne1).\]\[B_{\mathrm{end}}=Lq^n+PF,\qquad B_{\mathrm{start}}=Lq^n+PqF.\]

\(q=1\): both \(L+nP\). Extra factor \(q\): payments only.

Count the bounce event

Initial fall once; complete rebounds twice; peak’s current rise once. First landing: impact one.

\[D_{\mathrm{impact}\,n}=H+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}Hr^k.\]\[D_\infty=H+2\frac{Hr}{1-r}\quad(0<r<1).\]

For \(H>0\), no finite bounce reaches the limit.

Limits and linked equations

Positive increments \(c,cr,\ldots\) count once; \(0<r<1\).

\[D_\infty=\frac{c}{1-r},\qquad R_n=\frac{cr^n}{1-r}.\]

Least integer: preserve strictness; test the candidate and predecessor using decreasing gaps. Keep separate parameters and indices; identify each selection’s first term and ratio. After squaring, recheck original equations, signs, integer indices and convergence.
revision.checks:
• First value, count and event correct?
  • Deposit ages correct?
  • Bounce distances counted correctly?
  • Original equations checked; money rounded last?
